steps.detail: Identify primes dividing n and enforce their presence in m. Exclude primes conflicting with gcd(m+n, 210) = 1.
Remove primes 2, 3, 5, 7 from possible factors of n due to gcd restrictions.
Determine that n must contain a squared prime (≥11) since m isn't a multiple of n despite sharing prime factors.
Start with smallest squared primes (e.g., 11² = 121) and compute corresponding m values satisfying divisibility without full multiplicity.
Ensure m + n avoids forbidden primes and satisfies gcd conditions. Iterate over larger primes if initial candidates fail.

example.problem: Let \( m \) and \( n \) be positive integers satisfying the conditions
example.solution: Let \( m \) and \( n \) be positive integers where \( m^m \) is a multiple of \( n^n \) and \( m \) is not a multiple of \( n \). If a prime \( p \) divides \( n \), then \( p \) divides \( n^n \), so it also divides \( m^m \), and thus \( p \) divides \( m \). Therefore any prime \( p \) dividing \( n \) also divides both \( m \) and \( k = m + n \). Because \( k \) is relatively prime to \( 210 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \), the primes \( 2, 3, 5, \) and \( 7 \) cannot divide \( n \). Furthermore, because \( m \) is divisible by every prime factor of \( n \), but \( m \) is not a multiple of \( n \), the integer \( n \) must be divisible by the square of some prime, and that prime must be at least \( 11 \). Thus \( n \) must be at least \( 11^2 = 121 \). If \( n = 11^2 \), then \( m \) must be a multiple of \( 11 \) but not a multiple of \( 121 \), and \( m^m \) must be divisible by \( n^n = 121^{121} = 11^{242} \). Therefore \( m \) must be a multiple of \( 11 \) that is greater than \( 242 \). Let \( m = 11m_0 \), with \( m_0 > 22 \). Then \( k = m + n = 11(m_0 + 11) \). The least \( m_0 > 22 \) for which \( m_0 + 11 \) is not divisible by any of the primes \( 2, 3, 5, \) or \( 7 \) is \( m_0 = 26 \), giving the prime \( m_0 + 11 = 37 \). Hence the least possible \( k \) when \( n = 121 \) is \( k = 11 \cdot 37 = 407 \). It remains to consider other possible values for \( n \). If \( n = 13^2 = 169 \), then \( m \) must be divisible by \( 13 \) but not \( 169 \), and \( m^m \) must be a multiple of \( n^n = 169^{169} = 13^{338} \), so \( m > 338 \). Then \( k = m + n > 169 + 338 = 507 \). All other possible values for \( n \) have \( n \geq 242 \), and in this case \( m > n \geq 242 \), so \( k \geq 2 \cdot 242 = 484 \). Hence no greater values of \( n \) can produce lesser values for \( k \), and the least possible \( k \) is indeed \( 407 \).

name: Strongly Connected Orientation Counting
description: This template counts the number of strongly connected orientations of a complete undirected graph by subtracting invalid configurations where nodes have all edges directed inward or outward.
applicability: When analyzing tournaments (complete oriented graphs) with strong connectivity requirements
When counting valid edge orientations that maintain reachability between all node pairs
When dealing with problems involving exclusion of extreme degree violations in directed graphs

steps.detail: Compute the total number of possible orientations of all edges without constraints, which equals 2^(number of edges).
Determine configurations violating strong connectivity: nodes with indegree = total nodes - 1 or outdegree = total nodes - 1.
Calculate cases where one specific node has all edges incoming/outgoing: multiply node choices by remaining edge orientations (2^remaining_edges).
Account for overlapping cases where one node has all-in and another has all-out edges: subtract overcounted overlaps using inclusion-exclusion.
Combine adjustments: Total = Total_Orientations - (All_In_Cases + All_Out_Cases - Both_Cases).

example.problem: Five towns are connected by a system of roads. There is exactly one road connecting each pair of towns. Find the number of ways there are to make all the roads one-way in such a way that it is still possible to get from any town to any other town using the roads (possibly passing through other towns on the way).
example.solution: We use Claim 1 along with complementary counting. Then, the number of valid cases is the total \(2^{10}\) minus the cases in which there are towns with indegree or outdegree 5. Number of cases in which there is a node with indegree 5: \(5 \times 2^6\) 5 ways to choose which town has indegree 5 and for the remaining roads, they each have 2 possible statuses. Similarly, the number of cases in which there is a node with outdegree 5 is also \(5 \times 2^6\) The number of cases in which there is a node with indegree 5 and there is a node with outdegree 5: \(5 \times 4 \times 2^3\) Thus, answer = \(2^{10} - (5 \times 2^6 + 5 \times 2^6 - 5 \times 4 \times 2^3) = 544\).

name: Geometric Similarity Ratio Equating
description: Relates surface area and volume ratios between two similar solids created by a parallel cut, using geometric similarity properties to derive a common ratio.
applicability: A solid is divided by a plane parallel to its base, creating similar sub-solids
Ratios of surface areas and volumes between the sub-solids must be equal
Problems involving proportional scaling of dimensions in geometric shapes

steps.detail: Confirm that the cut creates similar shapes (e.g., cones or pyramids) due to parallelism, establishing a uniform scale factor across dimensions.
Let $ x $ represent the linear scale factor between the smaller and original solids. Areas scale as $ x^2 $, volumes as $ x^3 $.
Calculate total painted areas for both solids, accounting for exposed surfaces (e.g., subtract overlapping areas for the frustum).
Express both the surface area ratio and volume ratio in terms of $ x $, then equate them to solve for the unknown scale factor.
Substitute the solved $ x $ back into either ratio expression to determine $ k $, simplifying to lowest terms $ \frac{m}{n} $.

example.problem: A solid in the shape of a right circular cone is 4 inches tall and its base has a 3-inch radius. The entire surface of the cone, including its base, is painted. A plane parallel to the base of the cone divides the cone into two solids, a smaller cone-shaped solid \( C \) and a frustum-shaped solid \( F \), in such a way that the ratio between the areas of the painted surfaces of \( C \) and \( F \) and the ratio between the volumes of \( C \) and \( F \) are both equal to \( k \). Given that \( k = \frac{m}{n} \), where \( m \) and \( n \) are relatively prime positive integers, find \( m + n \).
example.solution: Our original solid \( V \) has surface area \( A_v = \pi r^2 + \pi r \ell \), where \( \ell \) is the slant height of the cone. Using the Pythagorean Theorem or Pythagorean Triple knowledge, we obtain \( \ell = 5 \) and lateral area \( A_{\ell} = 15\pi \). The area of the base is \( A_B = 3^2\pi = 9\pi \). \( V \) and \( C \) are similar cones, because the plane that cut out \( C \) was parallel to the base of \( V \). Let \( x \) be the scale factor between the original cone and the small cone \( C \) in one dimension. Because the scale factor is uniform in all dimensions, \( x^2 \) relates corresponding areas of \( C \) and \( V \), and \( x^3 \) relates corresponding volumes. Then, the ratio of the painted areas \( \frac{A_c}{A_f} \) is \( \frac{15\pi x^2}{9\pi + 15\pi - 15\pi x^2} = \frac{5x^2}{8 - 5x^2} = k \) and the ratio of the volumes \( \frac{V_c}{V_f} \) is \( \frac{x^3}{1 - x^3} = k \). Since both ratios are equal to \( k \), they are equal to each other. Therefore, \( \frac{5x^2}{8 - 5x^2} = \frac{x^3}{1 - x^3} \). Now we must merely solve for \( x \) and substitute back into either ratio. Cross multiplying gives \( 5x^2 (1 - x^3) = x^3 (8 - 5x^2) \). Dividing both sides by \( x^2 \) and distributing the \( x \) on the right, we have \( 5 - 5x^3 = 8x - 5x^3 \), and so \( 8x = 5 \) and \( x = \frac{5}{8} \). Substituting back into the easier ratio, we have \( \frac{\left( \frac{5}{8} \right)^3}{1 - \left( \frac{5}{8} \right)^3} = \frac{\frac{125}{512}}{\frac{387}{512}} = \frac{125}{387} \). And so we have \( m + n = 125 + 387 = 512 \).

name: Inclusion-Exclusion with Complementary Counting for Grid Colorings
description: This template calculates the probability of avoiding specific monochromatic substructures in a colored grid by combining complementary counting with inclusion-exclusion to handle overlapping cases.
applicability: When calculating probabilities involving colored grids with forbidden monochromatic substructures (e.g., 2x2 red squares)
When forbidden substructures can overlap, making direct counting difficult
When individual colorings are independent and equally likely

steps.detail: Compute total possible colorings as $ c^{n 	imes m} $ for $ c $ colors and grid size $ n 	imes m $.
Enumerate all possible positions of the forbidden substructure (e.g., all 2×2 blocks in a grid).
Count colorings with at least one forbidden substructure by multiplying the number of positions by remaining degrees of freedom (e.g., unforced cells).
Group intersections of multiple forbidden substructures by overlap complexity (e.g., adjacent vs. diagonal blocks).
Iteratively account for overlaps using inclusion-exclusion, alternating additions and subtractions based on intersection sizes.
Subtract complementary count (invalid configurations) from total to get valid configurations.

example.problem: Each unit square of a 3-by-3 unit-square grid is to be colored either blue or red. For each square, either color is equally likely to be used. The probability of obtaining a grid that does not have a 2-by-2 red square is \( \dfrac{m}{n} \), where \( m \) and \( n \) are relatively prime positive integers. Find \( m + n \).
example.solution:
We can use complementary counting, counting all of the colorings that have at least one red 2 \( 	imes \) 2 square.


- For at least one red 2 \( 	imes \) 2 square:

There are four 2 \( 	imes \) 2 squares to choose which one will be red. Then there are \( 2^5 \) ways to color the rest of the squares. \( 4 	imes 32 = 128 \)


- For at least two 2 \( 	imes \) 2 squares:

There are two cases: those with two 2x2 red squares on one side and those without red squares on one side but at two corners.

The first case is easy: 4 ways to choose which the side the squares will be on, and \( 2^3 \) ways to color the rest of the squares, so 32 ways to do that. For the second case, there will be only two ways to pick two squares, and \( 2^2 \) ways to color the other squares. \( 32 + 8 = 40 \)


- For at least three 2 \( 	imes \) 2 squares:

Choosing three such squares leaves only one square left, with four places to place it. This is \( 2 	imes 4 = 8 \) ways.


- For at least four 2 \( 	imes \) 2 squares, we clearly only have one way.

By the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion, there are (alternatively subtracting and adding) \( 128 - 40 + 8 - 1 = 95 \) ways to have at least one red 2 \( 	imes \) 2 square.

There are \( 2^9 = 512 \) ways to paint the 3 \( 	imes \) 3 square with no restrictions, so there are \( 512 - 95 = 417 \) ways to paint the square with the restriction. Therefore, the probability of obtaining a grid that does not have a 2 \( 	imes \) 2 red square is \( \dfrac{417}{512} \), and \( 417 + 512 = 929 \).

name: Divisor Decomposition for Structured Numbers
description: This template solves problems where a number's structure (e.g., fixed trailing digits) interacts with divisibility constraints. It combines algebraic decomposition, factor analysis, and systematic enumeration of valid divisors.
applicability: Numbers with fixed trailing digits whose prefixes must divide the full number
Problems requiring interaction between digit patterns and divisibility rules
Situations where prime factorization can constrain variable possibilities

steps.detail: Express the number in terms of its components (prefix and suffix). For example, write N = D * x + S where D is a power of 10 matching suffix length and S is the fixed suffix.
Factor common terms from the expression to identify relationships between variables. In the example, factor 20 from N = 10000x + 2020 to get N = 20(500x + 101).
Convert the requirement that prefix divides N into an algebraic condition. Here, force N/x to be integer, leading to constraints on x's factors.
Decompose x into coprime factors derived from the expression's constants. Use known prime factors (like 20's divisors and 101's primality) to enumerate valid cases systematically.
List all mathematically valid combinations while eliminating contradictions. Calculate required metrics (digit sums here) across all solutions.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the set of positive integers \(N\) with the property that the last four digits of \(N\) are 2020, and when the last four digits are removed, the result is a divisor of \(N\). For example, 42,020 is in \(S\) because 4 is a divisor of 42,020. Find the sum of all the digits of all the numbers in \(S\). For example, the number 42,020 contributes \(4 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 8\) to this total.
example.solution: Note that for all \(N \in S\), \(N\) can be written as \(N = 10000x + 2020 = 20(500x + 101)\) for some positive integer \(x\). Because \(N\) must be divisible by \(x\), \(\dfrac{20(500x + 101)}{x}\) is an integer. We now let \(x = ab\), where \(a\) is a divisor of 20. Then \(\dfrac{20(500x + 101)}{x} = \left(\dfrac{20}{a}\right)\left(\dfrac{500x}{b} + \dfrac{101}{b}\right)\). We know \(\dfrac{20}{a}\) and \(\dfrac{500x}{b}\) are integers, so for \(N\) to be an integer, \(\dfrac{101}{b}\) must be an integer. For this to happen, \(b\) must be a divisor of 101. 101 is prime, so \(b \in \{1, 101\}\). Because \(a\) is a divisor of 20, \(a \in \{1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20\}\). So \(x \in \{1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 101, 202, 404, 505, 1010, 2020\}\). Be know that all \(N\) end in 2020, so the sum of the digits of each \(N\) is the sum of the digits of each \(x\) plus \(2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 4\). Hence the sum of all of the digits of the numbers in \(S\) is \(12 \cdot 4 + 45 = 093\).

name: Inclusion-Exclusion for Strongly Connected Tournaments
description: This template counts the number of strongly connected orientations of a complete undirected graph by subtracting configurations violating strong connectivity via inclusion-exclusion.
applicability: When analyzing tournaments (complete oriented graphs) where every pair of nodes has a single directed edge
Need to ensure strong connectivity (every node reachable from every other)
Avoiding configurations with nodes acting as universal sinks (all edges incoming) or sources (all edges outgoing)

steps.detail: Calculate the total number of possible orientations of the graph, which is 2^(number of edges) since each edge can be directed independently.
Define 'bad' configurations as those containing at least one node with all edges directed inward (sink) or outward (source).
Subtract invalid configurations where any node is a sink/source, then adjust for overcounted overlaps where multiple forbidden subgraphs coexist.
Confirm that the absence of sinks/sources guarantees strong connectivity through cycle existence and reachability arguments.

example.problem: Five towns are connected by a system of roads. There is exactly one road connecting each pair of towns. Find the number of ways there are to make all the roads one-way in such a way that it is still possible to get from any town to any other town using the roads (possibly passing through other towns on the way).
example.solution: It is obvious that any configuration of one-way roads which contains a town whose roads all lead into it or lead out of it cannot satisfy the given. We claim that any configuration which does not have a town whose roads all lead into it or lead out of it does satisfy the given conditions. Now we show that a loop of 3 or more towns exist. Pick a town, then choose a neighboring town to travel to 5 times. Of these 6 towns visited, at least two of them must be the same; therefore there must exist a loop of 3 or more towns because a loop of 2 towns cannot exist. We want to show that the loop can be reached from any town, and any town can be reached from the loop.

name: Rhombus Incircle Distance Analysis
description: Analyzes distances from a point on a rhombus's incircle to its sides using geometric relationships, including distance summation, perpendicular constructions, and the geometric mean theorem to derive side lengths.
applicability: When a point lies on the incircle of a rhombus or parallelogram with known distances to multiple sides
When seeking to determine the perimeter or side length of a rhombus given incircle-related distance constraints
When geometric mean theorem or Pythagorean theorem applications are implied by perpendicular constructions

steps.detail: Use the property that the sum of distances from an internal point to two opposite sides of a rhombus equals the height (distance between those sides). This confirms the height of the rhombus.
Identify perpendicular segments from the point to sides and intersections with other lines. Use these to decompose the problem into manageable right triangles or segments.
For right triangles formed by projections, use the geometric mean theorem (altitude squared equals product of adjacent segments) to derive unknown lengths.
Calculate distances between key points using right triangles formed by projections and incircle radius constraints.
Combine derived lengths with the height to determine side length via trigonometric or proportional relationships, then compute perimeter.

example.problem: Rhombus \(ABCD\) has \(ngle BAD < 90^\circ\). There is a point \(P\) on the incircle of the rhombus such that the distances from \(P\) to the lines \(DA\), \(AB\), and \(BC\) are 9, 5, and 16, respectively. Find the perimeter of \(ABCD\).
example.solution: Using the diagram, since \(RT \perp AD\), \(FG \perp AB\), and \(E = AD \cap \omega\), \(E' = FG \cap AD\), \(RT = 9 + 16 = 25 = FG\) as heights of the rhombus. Since \(RP = QT = 9\), \(PQ = 16 - 9 = 7\), \(GE' = PF = 5\), \(PE' = 25 - 5 - 5 = 15\), and \(RE = \sqrt{RP \cdot RQ} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 16} = 12\), \(PE = \sqrt{RP^2 + RE^2} = 15\) implies \(E = E'\). Hence, the perimeter of the rhombus is \(\frac{125}{4} \cdot 4 = 125\).

name: Counting Unordered Integer Pairs via Stars and Bars
description: This template converts a problem requiring counting unordered integer pairs (r, q) with bounded sums into a combinatorial stars-and-bars framework, adjusting for overcounting by distinguishing symmetric and asymmetric cases.
applicability: Problems involving polynomials factorable into linear terms with integer coefficients
Counting distinct (a, b) pairs where a and b depend on symmetric properties of r and q
Situations where unordered pairs (r, q) map to unique outcomes despite ordered generation

steps.detail: Express coefficients (a, b) in terms of roots (r, q) using Vieta's identities: a = r + q, b = rq. Restrict r, q to non-negative integers based on problem constraints.

steps.step: Apply Stars and Bars for Ordered Counts
steps.detail: Model the sum constraint (e.g., 1 ≤ r + q ≤ N) as a stars-and-bars problem with slack variables. Compute total ordered pairs (r, q) using binomial coefficients, adjusting for invalid edge cases (e.g., subtracting configurations violating bounds).

Account for overcounting by splitting ordered pairs into symmetric (r = q) and asymmetric (r ≠ q) cases. Calculate symmetric pairs as those with even sums, then derive unordered count via (TotalOrdered - Symmetric)/2 + Symmetric.
Compute the result modulo the required base (e.g., 1000) after final adjustments.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the number of ordered pairs of integers \((a, b)\) with \(1 \leq a \leq 100\) and \(b \geq 0\) such that the polynomial \(x^2 + ax + b\) can be factored into the product of two (not necessarily distinct) linear factors with integer coefficients. Find the remainder when \(S\) is divided by 1000.
example.solution: Letting \(-r\) and \(-q\) be the roots, we must find the number of unordered pairs \((r, q)\) such that \(1 \leq r + q \leq 100\). To do this we define three boxes: \(r\), \(q\), and \(t\) for "trash." For example, if we had \(t = 77\), we would have any arrangement of \(r\) and \(q\) summing to \(23\). Note that we cannot have \(t = 100\), subtracting one from our total. By stars and bars, we have that the number of ordered pairs \((r, q)\) is \[ \binom{102}{2} - 1 = 5150. \] However, we are not done: we have double-counted cases such as \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 1)\) but not cases such as \((4, 4)\). Thus our answer will be \[ \frac{5150 - 50}{2} + 50 \pmod{100} = 600 \].

name: Volume via Adjacent Face Areas and Dihedral Angle
description: Calculates the volume of a tetrahedron using the areas of two adjacent faces, their shared edge length, and the dihedral angle between them.
applicability: Two adjacent triangular faces share a common edge
Known areas of both faces and length of the common edge
Known dihedral angle between the two faces

steps.detail: For each face, compute the height perpendicular to the common edge using area = (base × height)/2, where the base is the common edge.
Use the two computed heights and the dihedral angle to calculate the area of the triangle formed by these heights and the angle between them via the formula (a × b × sinθ)/2.
Express the cross-triangle's area as (base × height)/2, where the base is one of the previously computed heights, to solve for the tetrahedron's perpendicular height.
Apply the standard tetrahedron volume formula: (base area × height)/3, where the base area is one of the original face areas.

example.problem: In tetrahedron \(ABCD\), edge \(AB\) has length 3 cm. The area of face \(ABC\) is 15 cm\(^2\) and the area of face \(ABD\) is 12 cm\(^2\). These two faces meet each other at a 30\(^\circ\) angle. Find the volume of the tetrahedron in cm\(^3\).
example.solution: It is clear that \(DX = 8\) and \(CX = 10\) where \(X\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(D\) and \(C\) to side \(AB\). Thus \\[DXC] = \\frac{ab \\sin c}{2} = 20 = 5 \\cdot h \\to h = 4\) where \(h\) is the height of the tetrahedron from \(D\). Hence, the volume of the tetrahedron is \\frac{bh}{3} = 15 \\cdot \\frac{4}{3} = \boxed{020}\).

name: Cyclic Polygon Radius via Diameter and Ptolemy
description: This template solves for the radius of a circle circumscribing a polygon with known alternating side lengths by leveraging diameter assumptions, right triangle relationships, and Ptolemy’s theorem.
applicability: Polygon inscribed in a circle with alternating equal/consecutive sides
Need to find circumradius using geometric constraints
Presence of cyclic quadrilateral configurations within the polygon

steps.detail: Assume a diagonal spans a diameter, creating two right triangles via Thales’ theorem.
Express unknown leg lengths in terms of the diameter variable using Pythagorean theorem.
Set up an equation relating sides and diagonals in a cyclic quadrilateral derived from the polygon.
Square both sides to eliminate radicals, expand algebraically, and factorize to solve for diameter.
Halve the diameter solution and match to the target expression format $ p + \sqrt{q} $.

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: We know that \( AD = x \) is a diameter, hence \( \triangle ABD \) and \( \triangle ACD \) are right triangles. Let \( AB = BC = 22 \), and \( CD = 20 \). Hence, \( \triangle ABD \) is a right triangle with legs 22, \( \sqrt{x^2 - 484} \), and hypotenuse, \( x \), and \( \triangle ACD \) is a right triangle with legs 20, \( \sqrt{x^2 - 400} \), with hypotenuse \( x \). By Ptolemy's we have \[ 22(x + 20) = \sqrt{x^2 - 400} \sqrt{x^2 - 484} \] . We square both sides to get \[ 484(x + 20)^2 = (x^2 - 400)(x^2 - 484) \implies 484(x + 20) = (x - 20)(x^2 - 484) \implies 484x = x^3 - 20x^2 - 484x \implies x(x^2 - 20x - 968) = 0 \] We solve for \( x \) via the Quadratic Formula and receive \( x = 10 + 2 \sqrt{267} \), but we must divide by 2 since we want the radius, and hence \( 267 + 5 = \boxed{272} \).

name: Dynamic Programming for Circular Colorings
description: A dynamic programming approach to count valid colorings of a circular arrangement with adjacency constraints, leveraging symmetry to simplify calculations.
applicability: Problems involving coloring circular structures (e.g., rings, cycles) with adjacency restrictions
When symmetries allow fixing an initial choice to reduce computational complexity
Scenarios requiring efficient counting of permutations with local constraints

steps.detail: Assume a specific color for the first section to exploit symmetry, later scaling results by the total color count.
Let $ f(n, C_i) $ represent the number of valid colorings for the first $ n $ sections ending with color $ C_i $, ensuring no two adjacent colors match.

Use $ f(n, C_i) = \sum_{j 
eq i} f(n-1, C_j) $ to propagate valid colorings forward, excluding the current color $ C_i $ from prior positions.
Adjust final DP values to exclude invalid configurations where the last section matches the first (due to the ring structure).
Multiply computed values by the number of colors to account for all possible initial color choices omitted by the symmetry assumption.

example.problem: The figure below shows a ring made of six small sections which you are to paint on a wall. You have four paint colors available and you will paint each of the six sections a solid color. Find the number of ways you can choose to paint the sections if no two adjacent sections can be painted with the same color.
example.solution: Choose a section to start coloring. Assume, WLOG, that this section is color 1. We proceed coloring clockwise around the ring. Let \( f(n, C_i) \) be the number of ways to color the first \( n \) sections (proceeding clockwise) such that the last section has color \( C \). In general (except for when we complete the coloring), we see that\[ f(n, C_i) = \sum_{j \neq i} f(n-1, C_j), \]i.e., \( f(n, C_i) \) is equal to the number of colorings of \( n-1 \) sections that end in any color other than \( C_i \). Using this, we can compute the values of \( f(n, C) \) in the following table.\[\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} n & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 6 & 7 & 7 & 7 \\ 5 & 21 & 20 & 20 & 20 \\ 6 & 0 & 61 & 61 & 61 \\ \end{array}\]Note that \( f(6,1)=0 \) because then 2 adjacent sections are both color 1. We multiply this by 4 to account for the fact that the initial section can be any color. Thus the desired answer is \( (61+61+61)\cdot4 = \boxed{732}. \)

name: Prime Binary Encoding for Sequence Translation
description: This template transforms a multiplicative sequence involving primes into an additive binary-encoded sequence through bijective mapping of prime factors to binary digits.
applicability: When the sequence involves square-free numbers with prime factor modifications
When recurrence relations combine terms via prime multiplication/division
When direct computation of the sequence is intractable due to size

steps.detail: Verify that all terms in the sequence are square-free, ensuring unique prime factor combinations.
Assign each prime number to a binary digit position (e.g., 2→0th bit, 3→1st bit, 5→2nd bit, etc.).
Transform the original recurrence relation into a bitwise operation (e.g., multiplication → addition in binary).
Interpret the sequence index as a binary number encoding prime factors, enabling direct lookup of terms.

example.problem: For any integer \( k \geq 1 \), let \( p(k) \) be the smallest prime which does not divide \( k \). Define the integer function \( X(k) \) to be the product of all primes less than \( p(k) \) if \( p(k) > 2 \), and \( X(k) = 1 \) if \( p(k) = 2 \). Let \( \{ x_n \} \) be the sequence defined by \( x_0 = 1 \), and \( x_{n+1} X(x_n) = x_n p(x_n) \) for \( n \geq 0 \). Find the smallest positive integer \( t \) such that \( x_t = 2090 \).
example.solution:
Note that for any \( x_i \), for any prime \( p \), \( p^2 
mid x_i \). This provides motivation to translate \( x_i \) into a binary sequence \( y_i \).

Let the prime factorization of \( x_i \) be written as \( p_{a_1} \cdot p_{a_2} \cdot p_{a_3} \cdots \), where \( p_i \) is the \( i \)th prime number. Then, for every \( p_{a_k} \) in the prime factorization of \( x_i \), place a 1 in the \( a_k \)th digit of \( y_i \). This will result in the conversion \( x_1 = 2 \), \( x_2 = 3 \), \( x_3 = 2 * 3 = 6 \), \dots.

Multiplication for the sequence \( x_i \) will translate to addition for the sequence \( y_i \). Thus, we see that \( x_{n+1} X(x_n) = x_n p(x_n) \) translates into \( y_{n+1} = y_n + 1 \). Since \( x_0 = 1 \) and \( y_0 = 0 \), \( x_i \) corresponds to \( y_i \), which is \( i \) in binary. Since \( x_{10010101_2} = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 11 \cdot 19 = 2090 \), \( t = 10010101_2 =  oxed{149} \).

name: Trigonometric Approach to Cyclic Hexagon Radius
description: This template solves for the radius of a circle circumscribing a polygon with alternating side lengths by leveraging trigonometric relationships and geometric constraints.
applicability: Cyclic polygons with known side lengths and symmetric patterns
Problems requiring radius derivation in terms of radicals and integers
Geometric configurations involving central angles and perpendiculars

steps.detail: Relate each side length to its corresponding central angle using chord-length formula (e.g., chord = 2R sin(θ/2)).
Express sinθ in terms of sin(θ/2) and cos(θ/2) to connect adjacent geometric elements.
Identify perpendicular distances and hypotenuses to apply the Pythagorean theorem.
Derive a quadratic in R² by substituting trigonometric expressions into geometric constraints.
Use quadratic solutions to isolate R in the desired form (p + √q).

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: Let \( \angle AOB = \theta \). So, we have \( \sin \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{11}{r} \) and \( \cos \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{r^2 - 121}}{r} \). So, \[ \sin \theta = 2 \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{22 \sqrt{r^2 - 121}}{r^2} \]. Let \( H \) be the foot of the perpendicular from \( B \) to \( \overline{AD} \). We have \( BF = 2BH = 2r \sin \theta = \frac{44 \sqrt{r^2 - 121}}{r} \). Using Pythagorean theorem on \( \triangle BCF \), to get \( \left( \frac{44 \sqrt{r^2 - 121}}{r} \right)^2 + 20^2 = (2r)^2 \), or \( \frac{44^2 r^2 - 44^2 \cdot 121}{r^2} + 20^2 = 4r^4 \). Multiplying by \( r^2 \), we get \( 44^2 r^2 - 44^2 \cdot 121 + 20^2 r^2 = 4r^4 \). Rearranging and simplifying, we get a quadratic in \( r^2 \): \[ r^4 - 584r^2 + 242^2 = 0, \] which gives us \( r^2 = 292 \pm 10 \sqrt{267} \). Because \( r \) is in the form \( p + \sqrt{q} \), we know to choose the larger option, meaning \( r^2 = 292 + 10 \sqrt{267} \), so \( p \sqrt{q} = 5 \sqrt{267} \) and \( p^2 + q = 292 \). By inspection, we get \( (p, q) = (5, 267) \), so our answer is \( 5 + 267 = \boxed{272} \).

name: Maximizing Pairwise Sum Combinations
description: A method to determine the maximum possible value of the sum of two missing pairwise sums in a set of four numbers by leveraging total sum relationships and optimal combination selection.
applicability: When given six pairwise sums of four numbers with two missing values
When tasked with finding the maximum sum of the missing pairwise sums
When the problem involves combinatorial relationships between elements and their pairwise sums

steps.detail: Express the total sum of all elements (S) using the identity that the sum of all pairwise sums equals 3S.
Set up an equation connecting known sums, unknowns (x and y), and S: 3S = sum_of_known_sums + x + y.
Select the two largest known pairwise sums whose sum yields the maximum possible S, ensuring they represent disjoint element pairs.
Substitute the maximized S into the equation to solve for x + y = 3S - sum_of_known_sums.

example.problem: A set contains four numbers. The six pairwise sums of distinct elements of the set, in no particular order, are 189, 320, 287, 234, x, and y. Find the greatest possible value of x + y.
example.solution: Let the four numbers be \(a, b, c,\) and \(d\), in no particular order. Adding the pairwise sums, we have \(3a + 3b + 3c + 3d = 1030 + x + y\), so \(x + y = 3(a + b + c + d) - 1030\). Since we want to maximize \(x + y\), we must maximize \(a + b + c + d\). Of the four sums whose values we know, there must be two sums that add to \(a + b + c + d\). To maximize this value, we choose the highest pairwise sums, 320 and 287. Therefore, \(a + b + c + d = 320 + 287 = 607\). We can substitute this value into the earlier equation to find that \(x + y = 3(607) - 1030 = 1821 - 1030 = 791\).

name: Cyclic Polygon Radius Determination via Ptolemy's and Right Triangles
description: This template combines Ptolemy's Theorem on cyclic quadrilaterals and the Pythagorean Theorem from diameter-subtended right angles to derive the radius of a circumscribed circle around a symmetric polygon.
applicability: When dealing with cyclic polygons (especially irregular ones) with repeating side length patterns
Presence of a diameter that can form a right triangle with polygon sides
Symmetric configurations allowing formation of isosceles trapezoids or other cyclic quadrilaterals

steps.detail: Select four consecutive vertices forming a cyclic quadrilateral with exploitable symmetry or equal diagonals
Use the relationship between products of diagonals and sums of side products in cyclic quadrilaterals
Connect endpoints of a diameter to form a right triangle with known side lengths
Combine quadratic relationships from both theorems to isolate diameter/radius terms

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: Join the diameter of the circle \( AD \) and let the length be \( d \). By Ptolemy's Theorem on trapezoid \( ADEF \), \( (AD)(EF) + (AF)(DE) = (AE)(DF) \). Since it is an isosceles trapezoid, both diagonals are equal. Let them be equal to \( x \) each. Then \[ 20d + 22^2 = x^2 \] Since \( \angle AED \) is subtended by the diameter, it is right. Hence by the Pythagorean Theorem with right \( \triangle AED \): \[ (AE)^2 + (ED)^2 = (AD)^2 \] \[ x^2 + 22^2 = d^2 \] From the above equations, we have: \[ x^2 = d^2 - 22^2 = 20d + 22^2 \] \[ d^2 - 20d = 2 \times 22^2 \] \[ d^2 - 20d + 100 = 968 + 100 = 1068 \] \[ (d - 10) = \sqrt{1068} \] \[ d = \sqrt{1068} + 10 = 2 \times (\sqrt{267} + 5) \] Since the radius is half the diameter, it is \( \sqrt{267} + 5 \), so the answer is \( 5 + 267 \Rightarrow \boxed{272} \).

name: Complementary Counting with Inclusion-Exclusion for Circular Arrangements
description: Calculates valid configurations in circular arrangements by subtracting invalid adjacent-color violations using inclusion-exclusion, leveraging symmetry and combinatorial patterns.
applicability: Circular structures where adjacency wraps around (e.g., rings, cycles)
Constraints requiring no two adjacent elements to share properties (e.g., colors, values)
Overlapping forbidden conditions complicating direct enumeration

steps.detail: Compute all possible configurations without restrictions. For n sections and k colors, this is k^n.
Identify sets of configurations violating adjacency rules (e.g., Ai = colorings where border i has identical adjacent colors).
Exploit symmetry to calculate |Ai| and intersections: |Ai ∩ Aj ∩ ...| = k^(n - m), where m is the number of fixed overlaps.
Combine forbidden event counts with alternating signs for unions: Σ(-1)^(m+1) * C(total_borders, m) * k^(n - m).
Subtract PIE-computed invalid configurations from total to get valid count: Valid = Total - Invalid.

example.problem: The figure below shows a ring made of six small sections which you are to paint on a wall. You have four paint colors available and you will paint each of the six sections a solid color. Find the number of ways you can choose to paint the sections if no two adjacent sections can be painted with the same color.
example.solution: We use complementary counting. There are \( 4^6 \) total colorings of the ring without restriction. To count the complement, we wish to count the number of colorings in which at least one set of adjacent sections are the same color. There are six possible sets of adjacent sections that could be the same color (think of these as borders). Call these \( B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_6 \). Let \( \mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{A}_2, \ldots, \mathcal{A}_6 \) be the sets of colorings of the ring where the sections on both sides of \( B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_6 \) are the same color. We wish to determine \( |\mathcal{A}_1 \cup \mathcal{A}_2 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal{A}_6| \). Note that all of these cases are symmetric, and in general, \( |\mathcal{A}_i| = 4^5 \). There are 6 such sets \( \mathcal{A}_i \). Also, \( |\mathcal{A}_i \cup \mathcal{A}_j| = 4^4 \), because we can only change colors at borders, so if we have two borders along which we cannot change colors, then there are four borders along which we have a choice of color. There are \( \binom{6}{2} \) such pairs \( \mathcal{A}_i \cup \mathcal{A}_j \). Similarly, \( |\mathcal{A}_i \cup \mathcal{A}_j \cup \mathcal{A}_k| = 4^3 \), with \( \binom{6}{3} \) such triples, and we see that the pattern will continue for 4-tuples and 5-tuples. For 6-tuples, however, these cases occur when there are no changes of color along the borders, i.e., each section has the same color. Clearly, there are four such possibilities. Therefore, by PIE,\[ |\mathcal{A}_1 \cup \mathcal{A}_2 \cup \cdots \cup \mathcal{A}_6| = \binom{6}{1} \cdot 4^5 - \binom{6}{2} \cdot 4^4 + \binom{6}{3} \cdot 4^3 - \binom{6}{4} \cdot 4^2 + \binom{6}{5} \cdot 4^1 - 4. \]We wish to find the complement of this, or\[ 4^6 - \left( \binom{6}{1} \cdot 4^5 - \binom{6}{2} \cdot 4^4 + \binom{6}{3} \cdot 4^3 - \binom{6}{4} \cdot 4^2 + \binom{6}{5} \cdot 4^1 - 4 \right). \]By the Binomial Theorem, this is \( (4-1)^6 + 3 = \boxed{732}. \)

name: Parity-Constrained Divisor Pair Counting
description: This template counts integer solutions to equations like $x^2 - y^2 = N$ by analyzing divisor pairs of $N$ with parity constraints and combinatorial exponent distribution.
applicability: Equation can be factored into two integer variables (e.g., $x^2 - y^2 = ab$)
Factors must satisfy parity conditions (e.g., both even/odd)
Problem requires counting valid factorizations with sign variations

steps.detail: Decompose $N$ into its prime factors to analyze exponent distributions between the two factors.
Adjust allowable exponent ranges for primes (e.g., ensure each factor gets at least one power of 2 for evenness).
Use stars and bars to count ways to split exponents per prime while meeting constraints (e.g., $a + c = 	ext{exponent}$ with $a, c \geq 1$).
Multiply independent counts across all primes to get total valid positive divisor pairs.
Multiply by 2 if both positive and negative factor pairs yield distinct solutions (e.g., $(d,e)$ and $(-d,-e)$).

example.problem: A point whose coordinates are both integers is called a lattice point. How many lattice points lie on the hyperbola \( x^2 - y^2 = 2000^2 \)?
example.solution: As with solution 1, note that both \( x - y \) and \( x + y \) must have the same parities, meaning both have to be even. Additionally, we can express both of them in terms of \( 2^a \cdot 3^b \) and \( 2^c \cdot 3^d \). Now, \( a + c \) must be equal to 6, and both have to be greater than or equal to 1, so there are by stars and bars 7 ways to do this. Similarly, for \( b + d \), we have that both only need to be greater than or equal to 0, so this time there are 7 ways to do so. Since both can be negative, we multiply \( 7 \cdot 7 \cdot 2 \) which gives 098.

name: Symmetric Cyclic Polygon Radius Calculation
description: Exploits symmetry in cyclic polygons by analyzing midpoints and angles to derive trigonometric equations, enabling calculation of the circumradius.
applicability: Cyclic polygons with repeated/symmetric side lengths
Problems requiring circumradius expressed via radicals
Geometric configurations where midpoints form right triangles with the center

steps.detail: Assign labels to vertices to highlight repeating patterns, then isolate a representative substructure (e.g., half the polygon).

steps.step: Construct Midpoints and Connect to Center
steps.detail: Draw perpendicular bisectors from the center to midpoints of sides, creating right triangles for trigonometric analysis.
Define key angles using a single variable (e.g., θ), then express other angles and arcs in terms of this variable.
Relate side lengths to radius using sine/cosine ratios in right triangles (e.g., sinθ = opposite/hypotenuse).
Convert multi-angle expressions (e.g., cos2θ) into single-angle forms using identities to unify variables.
Substitute trigonometric terms into a polynomial framework, then solve for the radius using standard algebraic techniques.

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: Let us call the hexagon \( ABCDEF \), where \( AB = CD = DE = AF = 22 \), and \( BC = EF = 20 \). We can just consider one half of the hexagon, \( ABCD \), to make matters simpler. Draw a line from the center of the circle, \( O \), to the midpoint of \( BC \), \( X \). Now, draw a line from \( O \) to the midpoint of \( AB \), \( Y \). Clearly, \( \angle BXO = 90^\circ \), because \( BO = CO \), and \( \angle BYO = 90^\circ \), for similar reasons. Also notice that \( \angle AOX = 90^\circ \). Let us call \( \angle BOY = \theta \). Therefore, \( \angle AOB = 2\theta \), and so \( \angle BOX = 90 - 2\theta \). Let us label the radius of the circle \( r \). This means \[ \sin \theta = \frac{BY}{r} = \frac{11}{r} \] \[ \sin (90 - 2\theta) = \frac{BX}{r} = \frac{10}{r} \] Now we can use simple trigonometry to solve for \( r \). Recall that \( \sin (90 - \alpha) = \cos(\alpha) \). That means \( \sin (90 - 2\theta) = \cos 2\theta = \frac{10}{r} \). Recall that \( \cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2 \sin^2 \alpha \). That means \( \cos 2\theta = 1 - 2 \sin^2 \theta = \frac{10}{r} \). Let \( \sin \theta = x \). Substitute to get \( x = \frac{11}{r} \) and \( 1 - 2x^2 = \frac{10}{r} \). Now substitute the first equation into the second equation: \[ 1 - 2 \left( \frac{11}{r} \right)^2 = \frac{10}{r} \] Multiplying both sides by \( r^2 \) and reordering gives us the quadratic \[ r^2 - 10r - 242 = 0 \] Using the quadratic equation to solve, we get that \( r = 5 + \sqrt{267} \) (because \( 5 - \sqrt{267} \) gives a negative value), so the answer is \( 5 + 267 = \boxed{272} \).

name: Ordered Variable Assignment for Maximizing Pairwise Sums
description: This template organizes elements in descending order, assigns pairwise sums based on their relative magnitudes, and derives relationships between variables to compute unknown sums algebraically.
applicability: When given a complete or partially complete set of pairwise sums from four distinct elements
When tasked with maximizing or minimizing the sum of two unknown pairwise values
When logical deduction of variable relationships is feasible through ordering

steps.detail: Assume descending order (a > b > c > d) to establish hierarchy among elements.
Map largest sums to higher element pairs (e.g., a+b, a+c) and smallest to lower pairs (e.g., c+d).
Express unknown sums (x, y) in terms of known sums using substitutions derived from variable differences (e.g., a-b = (a+d)-(b+d)).
Combine equations to isolate x and y, leveraging additive relationships between assigned sums.

example.problem: A set contains four numbers. The six pairwise sums of distinct elements of the set, in no particular order, are 189, 320, 287, 234, x, and y. Find the greatest possible value of x + y.
example.solution: Note that if \(a > b > c > d\) are the elements of the set, then \(a + b > a + c > b + c\), \(a + d > b + d > c + d\). Thus we can assign \(a + b = x\), \(a + c = y\), \(b + c = 320\), \(a + d = 287\), \(b + d = 234\), \(c + d = 189\). Then \(x + y = (a + b) + (a + c) = [(a + d) - (b + d) + (b + c)] + [(a + d) - (c + d) + (b + c)]\).

name: Symmetry-Driven Ptolemy Application for Cyclic Polygons
description: Exploits rotational symmetry in cyclic polygons to decompose them into cyclic quadrilaterals, applies Ptolemy’s theorem for diagonal relationships, and solves resultant polynomial equations to determine circumradius.
applicability: Cyclic polygon with repeated/alternating side lengths suggesting rotational symmetry
Polygon can be bisected into congruent halves via a diameter
Need to compute circumradius through geometric-diophantine methods

steps.detail: Recognize rotational/reflectional symmetry in side lengths to identify bisection axis (diameter) splitting polygon into congruent halves
Project vertices onto diameter line to form right triangles, creating cyclic quadrilaterals with known side lengths and diagonals expressible via radius
Apply Ptolemy’s identity (product of diagonals = sum of opposite side products) to quadrilateral, substituting geometric expressions involving radius
Square both sides to eliminate radicals, organize terms into solvable polynomial equation in single variable (e.g., x representing horizontal projection)
Factor polynomial to discard extraneous roots (negative/zero physical lengths), solve remaining quadratic for positive real solutions matching geometric constraints

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: As we can see this image, it is symmetrical hence the diameter divides the hexagon into two congruent quadrilateral. Now we can apply the Ptolemy's theorem. Denote the radius is \( r \), we can get \[ 22 * 2x + 440 = \sqrt{4x^2 - 400} \sqrt{4x^2 - 484} \] , after simple factorization, we can get \[ x^4 - 342x^2 - 2420x = 0 \] , it is easy to see that \( x = -10 \), \( x = 0 \) are two solutions for the equation, so we can factorize that into \[ x(x + 10)(x^2 - 10x - 242) \] so we only need to find the solution for \[ x^2 - 10x - 242 = 0 \] and we can get \( x = (\sqrt{267} + 5) \) is the desired answer for the problem, and our answer is \( 5 + 267 \Rightarrow \boxed{272} \).

name: Lattice Point Enumeration with Pick's Theorem
description: Transforms combinatorial problems into geometric regions, using Pick's theorem to count lattice points efficiently.
applicability: When the problem can be modeled as counting integer lattice points within a geometric region
Especially applicable to polygons with vertices on integer coordinates
Useful for avoiding brute-force enumeration in structured counting problems

steps.detail: Map problem variables (e.g., integer pairs) to coordinates in a lattice plane.
Identify the polygonal region representing valid solutions based on constraints.
Calculate the number of lattice points lying exactly on the region's perimeter.
Use the formula Area = Interior Points + Boundary Points/2 - 1 to solve for unknown quantities.
Combine interior and boundary points, adjusting for invalid cases like excluded origin points.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the number of ordered pairs of integers \((a, b)\) with \(1 \leq a \leq 100\) and \(b \geq 0\) such that the polynomial \(x^2 + ax + b\) can be factored into the product of two (not necessarily distinct) linear factors with integer coefficients. Find the remainder when \(S\) is divided by 1000.
example.solution: Similar to the previous solution, we plot the triangle and cut it in half. Then, we find the number of boundary points, which is \(101 + 51 + 51 - 3\), or just \(200\). Using Pick's theorem, we know that the area of the half-triangle, which is \(2500\), is just \(I + 100 - 1\). That means that there are \(2401\) interior points, plus \(200\) boundary points, which is \(2601\). However, \((0, 0)\) does not work, so the answer is \[ 600. \]

name: Divisor Count and Parity-Based Sum Representation Analysis
description: Determines numbers expressible as sums of consecutive odd integers by linking divisor counts to valid sequences and considering parity constraints.
applicability: Problems requiring representation of numbers as sums of consecutive elements with parity constraints
Counting numbers with exactly k valid representations via divisor-based analysis
Scenarios where both odd/even parity of N and its divisors affect sequence validity

steps.detail: Express the sum of j consecutive odd integers starting at 2n+1 using arithmetic series formulas to derive N = j(2n + j)
Establish that j must divide N and impose non-negative integer constraints on n to determine bounds for j (j ≤ √N)

steps.step: Map Valid Representations to Divisor Counts
steps.detail: Relate the number of valid j values to the total divisors of N, accounting for parity restrictions on j (odd/even N requires odd/even j)
Determine possible prime factorization structures (e.g., p₁²p₂² or p₁p₂⁴) that yield the required number of divisors while respecting parity-specific constraints
Separately analyze odd and even N cases: For odd N, consider only odd divisors; for even N, substitute variables to transform into standard divisor analysis framework
List all numbers < limit satisfying derived prime factorization forms and parity-specific conditions through systematic case checking

example.problem: How many integers \( N \) less than 1000 can be written as the sum of \( j \) consecutive positive odd integers from exactly 5 values of \( j \geq 1 \)?
example.solution:
Let the first odd integer be \( 2n + 1 \), \( n \geq 0 \). Then the final odd integer is \( 2n + 1 + 2(j - 1) = 2(n + j) - 1 \). The odd integers form an arithmetic sequence with sum \( N = j \left(  rac{(2n + 1) + (2(n + j) - 1)}{2} ight) = j(2n + j) \). Thus, \( j \) is a factor of \( N \).

Since \( n \geq 0 \), it follows that \( 2n + j \geq j \) and \( j \leq \sqrt{N} \).

Since there are exactly 5 values of \( j \) that satisfy the equation, there must be either 9 or 10 factors of \( N \). This means \( N = p_1^2 p_2^2 \) or \( N = p_1 p_2^4 \). Unfortunately, we cannot simply observe prime factorizations of \( N \) because the factor \( (2n + j) \) does not cover all integers for any given value of \( j \).

Instead we do some casework:

- If \( N \) is odd, then \( j \) must also be odd. For every odd value of \( j \), \( 2n + j \) is also odd, making this case valid for all odd \( j \). Looking at the forms above and the bound of 1000, \( N \) must be

\( (3^2 \cdot 5^2),\ (3^2 \cdot 7^2),\ (3^4 \cdot 5),\ (3^4 \cdot 7),\ (3^4 \cdot 11) \)

Those give 5 possibilities for odd \( N \).

- If \( N \) is even, then \( j \) must also be even. Substituting \( j = 2k \), we get

\( N = 4k(n + k) \implies  rac{N}{4} = k(n + k) \)

Now we can just look at all the prime factorizations since \( (n + k) \) cover the integers for any \( k \). Note that our upper bound is now 250:

\(  rac{N}{4} = (2^2 \cdot 3^2), (2^2 \cdot 5^2), (2^2 \cdot 7^2), (3^2 \cdot 5^2), (2^4 \cdot 3), (2^4 \cdot 5), (2^4 \cdot 7), (2^4 \cdot 11), (2^4 \cdot 13), (3^4 \cdot 2) \)

Those give 10 possibilities for even \( N \).

The total number of integers \( N \) is \( 5 + 10 = 15 \).

name: Divisibility via Number Decomposition and Divisor Digit Summation
description: This template handles problems where a number has a fixed suffix and a variable prefix that must divide the entire number. It decomposes the number structurally, derives divisibility constraints on the prefix, enumerates valid prefixes via divisor analysis, and computes digit sums across all valid solutions.
applicability: Problems involving numbers with a fixed suffix (e.g., last four digits)
When a prefix portion of the number must divide the full number
Need to calculate total digit sums over all valid numbers
Structure allows separation into prefix×(power of 10) + suffix

steps.detail: Express the number as N = a * 10^k + b, where b represents the fixed suffix and a is the prefix requiring divisibility.
Use the property that a divides N implies a divides b, since a divides a * 10^k. Thus, a must be a divisor of b.
Find all positive integers a such that a divides b. Include constraints like a > 0 and a < N (if applicable).
For each valid a, compute the digit sum of N = a * 10^k + b by adding the digit sum of a and the digit sum of b.
Sum all digit contributions from every valid a, combining individual digit sums of a and multiplying the suffix's digit sum by the count of valid divisors.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the set of positive integers \(N\) with the property that the last four digits of \(N\) are 2020, and when the last four digits are removed, the result is a divisor of \(N\). For example, 42,020 is in \(S\) because 4 is a divisor of 42,020. Find the sum of all the digits of all the numbers in \(S\). For example, the number 42,020 contributes \(4 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 8\) to this total.
example.solution: We note that any number in \(S\) can be expressed as \(a(10,000) + 2,020\) for some integer \(a\). The problem requires that \(a\) divides this number, and since we know \(a\) divides \(a(10,000)\), we need that \(a\) divides 2020. Each number contributes the sum of the digits of \(a\), as well as \(2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 4\). Since 2020 can be prime factorized as \(2^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 101\), it has \((2 + 1)(1 + 1)(1 + 1) = 12\) factors. So if we sum all the digits of all possible \(a\) values, and add \(4 \cdot 12 = 48\), we obtain the answer. Now we list out all factors of 2,020, or all possible values of \(a\): 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 101, 202, 404, 505, 1010, 2020. If we add up these digits, we get 45, for a final answer of \(45 + 48 = 093\).

name: Cyclic Polygon Radius via Trapezoidal Decomposition
description: This template calculates the radius of a circle circumscribed around a symmetric cyclic polygon by analyzing a trapezoidal subfigure and applying the Pythagorean theorem.
applicability: Polygon inscribed in a circle with alternating equal side lengths
Presence of symmetrical structure suggesting trapezoidal decomposition
Need to relate radius to side lengths through geometric relationships

steps.detail: Locate a trapezoidal subfigure within the polygon using repetitive side lengths to establish parallel sides and symmetry.
Draw a perpendicular line from a vertex to the opposite base, creating a right triangle involving the circle's radius.
Express triangle legs using known side lengths and radius variables, then equate via Pythagorean identity.
Simplify the equation into standard quadratic form and solve for radius in the required algebraic expression.

example.problem: A hexagon that is inscribed in a circle has side lengths 22, 22, 20, 22, 22, and 20 in that order. The radius of the circle can be written as \( p + \sqrt{q} \), where \( p \) and \( q \) are positive integers. Find \( p + q \).
example.solution: Using the trapezoid \( ABCD \) mentioned above, draw an altitude of the trapezoid passing through point \( B \) onto \( AD \) at point \( J \). Now, we can use the Pythagorean theorem: \[ (22^2 - (r - 10)^2) + 10^2 = r^2. \] Expanding and combining like terms gives us the quadratic \[ r^2 - 10r - 242 = 0 \] and solving for \( r \) gives \( r = 5 + \sqrt{267} \). So the solution is \( 5 + 267 = \boxed{272} \).

name: Strongly Connected Orientation via Inclusion-Exclusion
description: This template calculates the number of strongly connected orientations in a complete undirected graph by systematically subtracting invalid configurations using inclusion-exclusion principles.
applicability: When counting valid orientations of a complete graph ensuring strong connectivity
Problems requiring elimination of unreachable node subsets
Scenarios involving combinatorial adjustments for overlapping invalid cases

steps.detail: Calculate all possible one-way assignments without connectivity constraints. For n nodes, compute 2^{C(n,2)} as the baseline.

Identify configurations where one node becomes unreachable. For each node, fix all edges incident to it as unidirectional (away from the excluded node), reducing available degrees of freedom. Multiply combinations: C(n,1)*2^{C(n-1,2)+n-1}.

Account for overlapping invalid cases by analyzing pairs of excluded nodes. Fix edges between excluded and included nodes as unidirectional, then compute residual configurations: C(n,2)*2^{C(n-2,2)+2(n-2)}.
Recognize equivalence between excluding k nodes and excluding (n-k) nodes due to directional duality. Stop inclusion-exclusion iterations at floor(n/2) to avoid overcounting.

example.problem: Five towns are connected by a system of roads. There is exactly one road connecting each pair of towns. Find the number of ways there are to make all the roads one-way in such a way that it is still possible to get from any town to any other town using the roads (possibly passing through other towns on the way).
example.solution: Assume the five towns are named A, B, C, D, and E. Draw roads that connect each of the five towns. First, figure out how many total roads there are with no restrictions. This would be \(2^{10}\), or 1024. Next, add together the number of restrictions (or incorrect cases) there are. One incorrect case happens if we can't get to one of the five towns. When that happens, any roads that connect that town with any of the other four towns must be one way. Four roads are invalidated (because they are one way) as, assuming we can't get to town A, roads AB, AC, AD, and AE would all be one way. Since there are \(\binom{5}{1}\) ways of choosing which town to restrict, there are \(5 \cdot 2^{10-4}\), or 320 restrictions in this case. The next case is when we can't get to two of the towns. Let's assume we don't want to get to towns A and B. Then, roads AC, AD, AE, BC, BD, and BE are all invalidated. Since there are \(\binom{5}{2}\) of choosing which two towns to restrict, there are \(10 \cdot 2^{10-6}\), or 160 restrictions in this case. Notice that when we restrict three towns, it is the same thing as restricting two towns. For example, if we restricted entry to towns C, D, and E from towns A and B, it's the same thing as if we restricted entry to towns A and B from towns C, D, and E, as the exact same roads are invalidated in both cases. Thus, our final answer is \(1024 - (320 + 160) = 544\) arrangements.

name: Integer Factorization via Coordinate Mapping
description: Transforms polynomial factorization constraints into a coordinate geometry problem, leveraging symmetry and systematic counting of lattice points to determine valid integer pairs.
applicability: Problems involving integer factorization of quadratics with bounded coefficients
Scenarios requiring enumeration of non-negative integer solutions to linear-diophantine constraints
Situations where symmetry simplifies combinatorial counting

steps.detail: Express polynomial coefficients as sums/products of new variables (e.g., a = c + d, b = cd for quadratic x² + ax + b).
Convert bounds on original variables (a, b) into inequalities for new variables (c, d), ensuring non-negativity and avoiding invalid cases.
Map variable relationships to a coordinate plane (c vs. d), identifying regions containing valid lattice points under constraints.
Exploit symmetry across lines like y = x to avoid double-counting, focusing on triangular or trapezoidal subregions.
Break complex regions into simpler shapes (e.g., triangles, trapezoids) and compute counts via arithmetic series formulas.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the number of ordered pairs of integers \((a, b)\) with \(1 \leq a \leq 100\) and \(b \geq 0\) such that the polynomial \(x^2 + ax + b\) can be factored into the product of two (not necessarily distinct) linear factors with integer coefficients. Find the remainder when \(S\) is divided by 1000.
example.solution: Let the linear factors be \((x + c)(x + d)\). Then, \(a = c + d\) and \(b = cd\). We know that \(1 \leq a \leq 100\) and \(b \geq 0\), so \(c\) and \(d\) both have to be non-negative. However, \(a\) cannot be \(0\), so at least one of \(c\) and \(d\) must be greater than \(0\), i.e. positive. Also, \(a\) cannot be greater than \(100\), so \(c + d\) must be less than or equal to \(100\). Essentially, if we plot the solutions, we get a triangle on the coordinate plane with vertices \((0, 0)\), \((0, 100)\), and \((100, 0)\). Remember that \((0, 0)\) does not work, so there is a square with the top right corner \((1, 1)\). Note that \(c\) and \(d\) are interchangeable since they end up as \(a\) and \(b\) in the end anyways. Thus, we simply draw a line from \((1, 1)\) to \((50, 50)\), designating one of the halves as our solution (since the other side is simply the coordinates flipped). We note that the pattern from \((1, 1)\) to \((50, 50)\) is \(2 + 3 + 4 + \dots + 51\) solutions and from \((51, 49)\) to \((100, 0)\) is \(50 + 49 + 48 + \dots + 1\) solutions, since we can decrease the \(y\)-value by \(1\) until \(0\) for each coordinate. Adding up gives \[ \frac{2 + 51}{2} \cdot 50 + \frac{50 + 1}{2} \cdot 50. \] This gives us \(2600\), and \(2600 \equiv 600 \mod 1000\).

name: Integer Partition Counting for Quadratic Factorization
description: Translates the count of factorable quadratics into a combinatorial problem of partitioning integers $a$ into two non-negative integers $c, d$, then computes the total using summation techniques.
applicability: When needing to count the number of quadratics $x^2 + ax + b$ with integer coefficients that factor into linear terms.
When $a$ and $b$ have explicit bounds.
When the roots must be integers (not just rational).

steps.detail: Express the quadratic as $(x + c)(x + d)$ where $c, d$ are non-negative integers. Relate $a = c + d$ and $b = cd$.
Translate bounds on $a$ and $b$ into constraints on $c$ and $d$. For example, $1 \leq a \leq N$ becomes $1 \leq c + d \leq N$.
Recognize that each unordered pair $\{c, d\}$ corresponds to a unique $(a, b)$ pair due to distinct products $cd$ for fixed $a$.
Fix one variable (e.g., $c$) and express the other ($d$) in terms of $c$ to simplify counting valid combinations.
Compute the total number of valid pairs using arithmetic progressions or direct summation, accounting for symmetry (e.g., $c \leq d$).
Subtract invalid cases (e.g., $c = d = 0$ when $a = 0$) to ensure constraints are strictly met.

example.problem: Let \(S\) be the number of ordered pairs of integers \((a, b)\) with \(1 \leq a \leq 100\) and \(b \geq 0\) such that the polynomial \(x^2 + ax + b\) can be factored into the product of two (not necessarily distinct) linear factors with integer coefficients. Find the remainder when \(S\) is divided by 1000.
example.solution: Let's say that the quadratic \(x^2 + ax + b\) can be factored into \((x + c)(x + d)\) where \(c\) and \(d\) are non-negative numbers. We can't have both of them zero because \(a\) would not be within bounds. Also, \(c + d \leq 100\). Assume that \(c < d\). \(d\) can be written as \(c + x\) where \(x \geq 0\). Therefore, \(c + d = 2c + x \leq 100\). To find the amount of ordered pairs, we must consider how many values of \(x\) are possible for each value of \(c\). The amount of possible values of \(x\) is given by \(100 - 2c + 1\). The \(+1\) is the case where \(c = d\). We don't include the case where \(c = d = 0\), so we must subtract a case from our total. The amount of ordered pairs of \((a, b)\) is: \[ \left( \sum_{c=0}^{50} (100 - 2c + 1) \right) - 1 \] This is an arithmetic progression. \[ \frac{(101 + 1)(51)}{2} - 1 = 2601 - 1 = 2600 \] When divided by \(1000\), it gives the remainder \(600\).

name: Obtuse Triangle Area Interval Analysis
description: Determines the range of areas for which all obtuse triangles with fixed side lengths are congruent by analyzing geometric constraints and overlapping regions.
applicability: Problems involving triangles with fixed side lengths and area constraints
Finding intervals where uniqueness (congruence) of triangles is guaranteed
Applications requiring combination of triangle inequality and trigonometric area formulas

steps.detail: Determine valid range for the third side based on given side lengths.
Use Pythagorean inequalities to split the third side range into intervals where different angles are obtuse.

steps.step: Express Area in Terms of Included Angle
steps.detail: Calculate area using formula $ \frac{1}{2}ab\sin\theta $, where $ \theta $ is the angle between known sides.

steps.step: Analyze Area Ranges for Each Case
steps.detail: Determine the minimum and maximum possible areas for each obtuse configuration by evaluating bounds of $ \sin\theta $.
Identify intervals of area where only one triangle configuration exists to ensure congruence.

example.problem: For positive real numbers \(s\), let \(\tau(s)\) denote the set of all obtuse triangles that have area \(s\) and two sides with lengths 4 and 10. The set of all \(s\) for which \(\tau(s)\) is nonempty, but all triangles in \(\tau(s)\) are congruent, is an interval \([a, b]\). Find \(a^2 + b^2\).
example.solution: We start by defining a triangle. The two small sides MUST add to a larger sum than the long side. We are given 4 and 10 as the sides, so we know that the 3rd side is between 6 and 14, exclusive. We also have to consider the word OBTUSE triangles. That means that the two small sides squared is less than the 3rd side. So the triangles' sides are between 6 and \(\sqrt{84}\) exclusive, and the larger bound is between \(\sqrt{116}\) and 14, exclusive. The area of these triangles are from 0 (straight line) to \(2\sqrt{84}\) on the first "small bound" and the larger bound is between 0 and 20. \(0 < s < 2\sqrt{84}\) is our first equation, and \(0 < s < 20\) is our 2nd equation. Therefore, the area is between \(\sqrt{336}\) and \(\sqrt{400}\), so our final answer is \(\boxed{736}\).

name: Generating Function with Roots of Unity for Circular Coloring
description: This template models circular coloring problems with adjacency constraints by encoding valid transitions as polynomial terms and uses roots of unity to extract counts satisfying modular closure conditions.
applicability: Counting colorings on circular arrangements where adjacent elements must differ
Problems requiring modular consistency across cyclic boundaries
Situations with symmetric state transitions and periodic boundary conditions

steps.detail: Represent valid color transitions between adjacent sections as polynomial terms where exponents correspond to color differences modulo the number of colors.
Raise the transition polynomial to the power of the number of sections to model all sequential transitions around the cycle.
Use roots of unity to isolate coefficients where the total exponent satisfies the modular closure condition required for cyclic consistency.
Average evaluations of the generating function at all roots of unity and scale by the number of possible starting states.

example.problem: The figure below shows a ring made of six small sections which you are to paint on a wall. You have four paint colors available and you will paint each of the six sections a solid color. Find the number of ways you can choose to paint the sections if no two adjacent sections can be painted with the same color.
example.solution: We use generating functions. Suppose that the colors are \( 0, 1, 2, 3 \). Then as we proceed around a valid coloring of the ring in the clockwise direction, we know that between two adjacent sections with colors \( s_i \) and \( s_{i+1} \), there exists a number \( d_i \in \{1, 2, 3\} \) such that \( s_{i+1} \equiv s_i + d_i \pmod{4} \). Therefore, we can represent each border between sections by the generating function \( (x + x^2 + x^3) \), where \( x, x^2, x^3 \) correspond to increasing the color number by \( 1, 2, 3 \pmod{4} \), respectively. Thus the generating function that represents going through all six borders is \( A(x) = (x + x^2 + x^3)^6 \), where the coefficient of \( x^n \) represents the total number of colorings where the color numbers are increased by a total of \( n \) as we proceed around the ring. But if we go through all six borders, we must return to the original section, which is already colored. Therefore, we wish to find the sum of the coefficients of \( x^n \) in \( A(x) \) with \( n \equiv 0 \pmod{4} \). Now we note that if \( P(x) = x^n \), then\[ P(x) + P(ix) + P(-x) + P(-ix) = \begin{cases} 4x^n & \text{if } n \equiv 0 \pmod{4} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]Therefore, the sum of the coefficients of \( A(x) \) with powers congruent to \( 0 \pmod{4} \) is\[ \frac{A(1) + A(i) + A(-1) + A(-i)}{4} = \frac{3^6 + (-1)^6 + (-1)^6 + (-1)^6}{4} = \frac{732}{4}. \]We multiply this by 4 to account for the initial choice of color, so our answer is \boxed{732}.

name: Circular Arrangement Coloring Recursion
description: Solves circular arrangement coloring problems by recursive case analysis based on relationships between adjacent/previous elements.
applicability: Problems involving circular arrangements where adjacent elements cannot share colors
When recurrence relations can be derived through case analysis of element relationships
Scenarios requiring preservation of constraints across circular boundaries

steps.detail: Determine initial values for small instances of the problem (e.g., n=1,2,3) through direct enumeration.
Split the problem into subcases based on the relationship between current and previous elements (same/different color).
Calculate configurations where the (n-1)th element matches the first element's color, reducing degrees of freedom for nth element.
Calculate configurations where the (n-1)th element differs from the first element's color, maintaining distinct constraints for nth element.
Combine subcase results into a recurrence relation that expresses C(n) in terms of smaller instances C(n-1), C(n-2), etc.
Apply the recurrence relation iteratively starting from base cases to solve for the target instance size.

example.problem: The figure below shows a ring made of six small sections which you are to paint on a wall. You have four paint colors available and you will paint each of the six sections a solid color. Find the number of ways you can choose to paint the sections if no two adjacent sections can be painted with the same color.
example.solution: We will take a recursive approach to this problem. We can start by writing out the number of colorings for a circle with 1, 2, and 3 compartments, which are 4, 12, and 24. Now we will try to find a recursive formula, \( C(n) \), for a circle with an arbitrary number of compartments \( n \). We will do this by focusing on the \( n-1 \) section in the circle. This section can either be the same color as the first compartment, or it can be a different color as the first compartment. We will focus on each case separately. Case 1: If they are the same color, we can say there are \( C(n-2) \) to fill the first \( n-1 \) compartments. The \( n \)th compartment must be different from the first and second to last compartments, which are the same color. Hence this case adds \( 3 \cdot C(n-2) \) to our recursive formula. Case 2: If they are different colors, we can say that there are \( C(n-1) \) to fill the first \( n-1 \) compartments, and for the the \( n \)th compartment, there are 2 ways to color it because the \( n-1 \) and 1 compartments are different colors. Hence this case adds \( 2 \cdot C(n-1) \). So our recursive formula, \( C(n) \), is \( 3 \cdot C(n-2) + 2 \cdot C(n-1) \). Using the initial values we calculated, we can evaluate this recursive formula up to \( n=6 \). When \( n=6 \), we get \boxed{732} valid colorings. (Solution by NeeNeeMath)

name: Circular Coloring Case Analysis
description: This template solves circular coloring problems with adjacency constraints by analyzing cases based on fixed reference positions and recursively computing valid configurations.
applicability: Problems involving coloring rings or circular arrays with adjacency restrictions
When rotational symmetry creates overlapping constraints between positions
Scenarios requiring systematic handling of repeated pattern constraints

steps.detail: Assign sequential labels to positions to establish clear adjacency relationships

steps.step: Select Alternating Positions for Case Basis
