name: Guaranteed Values for Covering and Matching on Graphs
description: Abstract practical problems into graph problems: tournament scheduling is equivalent to finding the minimum cardinality of a maximal set of edge-disjoint perfect matchings (1-factorization) of a complete graph; the erasure constraint is equivalent to the covering guarantee of 'greedily selecting by degree and deleting conflicting neighbors' at each step on a conflict graph. Key conclusions: the size of the minimum maximal matching set in a complete graph takes 'half-pairs' or 'half-pairs plus one' depending on the parity of the vertex count; conflict graphs containing odd cycle structures tighten the greedy guarantee. Upper bound uses the sufficient condition for the remaining graph to have no perfect matching (splitting into two odd components); lower bound uses 1-factorization construction; greedy selection proceeds by degree from large to small. Common errors: parity of vertex count causing formula boundary errors; omitting the correspondence between 'each pair plays at most once' and edge-disjoint matchings; conflicts only occur between two objects whose pairings are opposite numbers. Final step-by-step results: for K_{2n}, minimum maximal matching set takes n+1 when n is even, and n when n is odd (n=20→21); construction makes the complement of the union split into two odd components, with small examples K₄→3, K₆→3, K₈→5 for calibration; what is sought is 'maximum number of rounds where the tournament may terminate' = n+1 type, not the complete tournament rounds 2n−1. Conflict graph erasure guarantee: greedily select numbers by degree and delete conflicting neighbors; odd cycles ensure at most 2 points per three pairs.
applicability: Tournament scheduling problems abstracted to edge-disjoint perfect matchings on complete graphs
Erasure constraints modeled as greedy covering on conflict graphs
Problems where conflicts only occur between pairings that are opposite numbers
Determining the maximum number of rounds before a tournament may terminate
Cases requiring parity-based distinction for vertex counts in complete graphs

steps.step: Abstract the problem into a graph model
steps.detail: Map the tournament scheduling to a complete graph K_{2n} where vertices represent teams and edges represent matches. The constraint 'each pair plays at most once' corresponds to edge-disjoint matchings. Conflicts only occur between two objects whose pairings are opposite numbers, forming a conflict graph.

The problem asks for the maximum number of rounds where the tournament may terminate (i.e., the minimum cardinality of a maximal set of edge-disjoint perfect matchings), NOT the complete tournament rounds 2n−1.
For complete graph K_{2n}, the minimum maximal matching set size depends on the parity of n: if n is even, take n+1; if n is odd, take n. Calibration: n=20 (even)→21.

Use small complete graphs to calibrate: K₄→3, K₆→3, K₈→5. The construction ensures the complement of the union splits into two odd components, which is the sufficient condition for the remaining graph to have no perfect matching.

steps.step: Handle conflict graph erasure with greedy strategy
steps.detail: On the conflict graph, at each step greedily select by degree and delete conflicting neighbors. If the conflict graph contains odd cycle structures, the guarantee tightens: at most 2 points per three pairs.
Use 1-factorization construction to establish the lower bound for the minimum maximal matching set.

name: Worst-case grid extremal query and covering histogram
description: Two classes of worst-case extremal problems on grids/boards: (1) Determine the minimum number of queries required to uniquely identify a hidden structure under any possible answer pattern. Provide an explicit query scheme and prove a lower bound by constructing two configurations that are indistinguishable under two different answer patterns. (2) Place large square tiles on a board to maximize the highest frequency in the coverage-count histogram. First tile the main region with non-overlapping tiles (coverage value 1), then incrementally add tiles along boundary strips to balance newly added coverage against overlap, with fine-tuning at corners. Caveats: avoid redundant/overlapping queries; do not double-count boundary corner regions; empty cells with coverage value 0 are excluded from the histogram statistics.
applicability: Worst-case identification of a hidden structure on a grid/board via queries
Maximizing the most frequent coverage count when placing large square tiles on a board

steps.detail: Design a query set that uniquely determines the hidden structure under any answer pattern. A representative pattern is 'full-layer query plus odd-column supplementary query on adjacent faces', yielding a count of the form 324 + 162 = 486. Ensure the scheme avoids unnecessary redundancy and overlap among queries.

Prove the query lower bound by an information-theoretic indistinguishability argument: construct two distinct configurations and two answer patterns such that the configurations cannot be distinguished under those patterns, thereby showing any correct strategy must use at least the stated number of queries.

For the covering histogram problem, first cover the main region with non-overlapping large square tiles. The number of tiles is given by the parameterized closed form ⌊n/k⌋², where n is the board dimension and k is the tile side length. Every cell in this region receives coverage value 1.

Along the two boundary strips, incrementally add tiles to maximize the highest histogram frequency. Balance the gain from newly covered cells against the loss from overlapping coverage. Apply fine-tuning adjustments at corner regions to avoid double counting. Note that empty cells with coverage value 0 are not included in the histogram statistics.

name: Line Separation of Bichromatic Point Sets
description: Given a configuration of red and blue marked points in the plane, the problem is to partition the plane into regions using straight lines that do not pass through any marked point, such that each region contains points of only one color. The minimum number of lines required for any red-blue point configuration equals the number of points in the smaller color class. The upper bound is established by a sweep construction: project points onto a direction, sort them, and draw a line between each adjacent pair of opposite colors. The lower bound is established by a narrow-strip configuration where red and blue points strictly alternate, forcing a new line at every color switch. Caution: lines must not pass through marked points; the equivalence between 'no region contains both colors' and 'separating every adjacent opposite-color pair' must be proved completely. When a coarse region-counting argument conflicts with the alternating construction, trust the lower bound given by the alternating construction.
applicability: Any finite configuration of red and blue marked points in the plane
Separating lines must not pass through any marked point
Each resulting region must contain points of only one color
The minimum number of lines equals min(|red|, |blue|)

steps.detail: The minimum number of lines required is min(|red|, |blue|), i.e., the number of points in the smaller color class.

steps.step: Upper bound construction via projection sorting
steps.detail: Choose a projection direction such that all points have distinct projected coordinates. Sort the points along this direction. Scan the sorted sequence and, whenever two adjacent points have opposite colors, draw a straight line separating them. Since no line passes through a marked point and each adjacent opposite-color pair is separated, every region contains only one color. The number of lines used is at most the number of color changes, which is bounded by the size of the smaller color class.

steps.step: Lower bound construction via alternating narrow strips
steps.detail: Construct a configuration where red and blue points are placed in a narrow strip such that their order along the strip strictly alternates (e.g., R, B, R, B, ...). In this arrangement, each color switch requires a separate separating line because a single line cannot separate two non-consecutive switches in the alternating sequence. This forces at least min(|red|, |blue|) lines, matching the upper bound.

steps.step: Handle conflicts with coarse region counting
steps.detail: If a rough region-counting argument (e.g., counting maximum regions produced by k lines) yields a lower bound that conflicts with the alternating-strip construction, trust the lower bound given by the alternating construction, as it is a concrete adversarial configuration.

Ensure no separating line passes through a marked point. Do not assume without rigorous proof that 'no region contains both colors' is equivalent to 'separating every adjacent opposite-color pair' in the projected order; the equivalence must be established completely.

name: Row-Column Degree Constraints and Poset Extremal Arguments
description: A strategy for two related families of extremal problems. The first family encodes constraints as row-count/column-count pairing uniqueness and degree-sequence feasibility conditions (Gale–Ryser type dual inequalities). From pairing uniqueness one derives linear constraints, then tightens them to exact extremal values and proves attainability by explicit construction. The second family arranges objects into a matrix and uses poset chains together with the pigeonhole principle to prove that a crossing structure must appear; the critical threshold is on the order of the product of row and column dimensions plus one. After fixing the monotone direction of the poset, construct critical counterexamples and examples using the 'common-order multiple' method. Common pitfalls: confusing 'there exist two rows each with m entries' with 'every row has exactly m entries'; omitting the poset monotone direction (increasing/decreasing), which invalidates the pigeonhole argument; and reversing the direction of the dual inequalities. A key calibration: 'two rows of the same degree m ⇒ their column-sum sets are disjoint ⇒ 2m ≤ n' is only the first constraint. One must further apply a compressed-matrix inequality of the form a·n_a ≤ n to tighten the bound to the order m = n/2 − 4, and give an explicit construction where the remaining rows' degrees traverse the remaining values. For a two-interval family with total count t², the connectivity critical value is t(t−1)+1; the answer to report is the product plus one, not t itself.
applicability: Problems where row/column count pairing uniqueness yields linear constraints and Gale–Ryser type dual inequalities
Extremal problems requiring tightening of initial bounds via compressed-matrix inequalities such as a·n_a ≤ n
Matrix-arrangement problems where a crossing structure must be forced via poset chains and the pigeonhole principle
Connectivity thresholds for two-interval families of total size t², where the critical value is t(t−1)+1

steps.step: Write the relations between row and column counting statistics
steps.detail: Translate the problem constraints into equations or inequalities involving row counts and column counts. If pairing is unique, use it to derive linear constraints. For degree-sequence feasibility, write the Gale–Ryser type dual inequalities carefully, checking their direction.
If there exist two rows each of degree m, then their column-sum sets are disjoint, giving 2m ≤ n. Treat this as only the initial bound; do not stop here.

Apply inequalities of the form a·n_a ≤ n (where a is a degree value and n_a is the number of rows/columns with that degree) to compress the matrix and tighten the extremal bound. For example, this can tighten the bound to the order m = n/2 − 4.

steps.step: Construct explicit examples to show attainability
steps.detail: Give an explicit construction achieving the tightened bound. Let the remaining rows' degrees traverse the remaining available values, ensuring all constraints are satisfied.

steps.step: For matrix-poset crossing problems, fix the monotone direction and apply the pigeonhole principle
steps.detail: Arrange the objects into a matrix. Determine whether the poset monotone direction is increasing or decreasing (omitting this invalidates the argument). Use chain decomposition and the pigeonhole principle to prove that a crossing structure must appear once the number of objects exceeds the critical threshold, which is on the order of the product of row and column dimensions plus one.

steps.step: Use the common-order multiple method to build critical examples
steps.detail: After the poset monotone direction is fixed, construct critical counterexamples and positive examples by aligning elements along common-order multiples, demonstrating that the threshold is sharp.

steps.step: Report the correct critical value for two-interval families
steps.detail: For a two-interval family with total count t², the connectivity critical value is t(t−1)+1. Report the answer as the product plus one, not as t itself.

name: Binary Invariant: Population Count Conservation and Power-Sum Merging
description: In numerical games, invariants are often hidden in binary representations: for merging-type processes (each step takes equal amounts from two piles and merges them into a new pile), if the total number is not a power of 2, at least two non-empty piles remain, corresponding to power-sum decomposition; in erasing/merging-type games, the number of remaining items at termination equals the number of 1s in the binary representation of the initial total (conserved under optimal strategy). Solution route: first analyze the binary characteristics of the initial quantity (number of 1s, whether it is a power of 2); then prove each operation preserves this characteristic. Common pitfalls: merging operations require taking equal amounts from two piles; when not fully merged, the remaining structure differs; the argument for conservation of 'number of 1s in binary of sum' and 'remaining count' must cover both sides under optimal strategy. Step-by-step conclusion: For the game of erasing two numbers and writing their sum starting from N copies of 1, the guaranteed value = popcount(N) (the number of 1s in binary, e.g., N=1997→11111001101→8); one side maintains that the binary representations of all numbers have no common bits pairwise, while the other side pairs and merges according to power-sum decomposition; first compute popcount to determine the candidate, then complete the two-sided strategy loop.
applicability: Merging-type processes where each step takes equal amounts from two piles and merges them into a new pile
Erasing/merging-type games where two numbers are erased and their sum is written
Games starting from N copies of 1 where the total is not necessarily a power of 2
Scenarios requiring analysis of binary characteristics (number of 1s, power-of-2 status) of the initial quantity

steps.step: Analyze binary characteristics of the initial total quantity
steps.detail: Compute the binary representation of the initial total N. Count the number of 1s (popcount). Determine whether N is a power of 2. For example, N=1997 has binary representation 11111001101, which contains 8 ones, so popcount(1997)=8.

In erasing/merging-type games where two numbers are erased and their sum is written, the number of remaining items at termination equals the number of 1s in the binary representation of the initial total. This value is conserved under optimal play by both sides.

steps.step: Prove operation preserves the binary invariant
steps.detail: Show that each merging operation (taking equal amounts from two piles) or erasing-and-writing-sum operation preserves the popcount invariant. For merging processes, if the total is not a power of 2, at least two non-empty piles remain, corresponding to the power-sum decomposition of the total.

One side maintains that all numbers on the board have pairwise disjoint binary representations (no common bits). The other side pairs numbers according to power-sum decomposition and merges them. First compute popcount(N) to determine the guaranteed value candidate, then complete the strategy loop for both sides to establish the bound.

Merging operations require taking equal amounts from two piles; when piles are not fully merged, the remaining structure differs from the fully merged case. The conservation argument for 'number of 1s in binary of sum' and 'remaining count' must explicitly cover optimal strategies for both players.

name: Recursive Counting on Path Structures
description: When counting 'strictly increasing sequences' or 'independent sets' on paths or chessboards, use recurrences: the independent-set polynomial along path nodes satisfies a first-order linear recurrence (binary choice of not selecting/selecting the current node; if selected, the predecessor cannot be selected). Chessboard path counting can use snake/spiral filling so that each cell has at most one incoming edge and one outgoing edge, reducing the counting to counting sources (local minima) of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The recurrence must clearly state initial conditions (empty graph, single-vertex case). The goal of the filling construction is to make the number of 'local-minimum starting points' reach the theoretical lower bound. Common mistakes: omitting the 'if current point is selected, predecessor cannot be selected' constraint in the independent-set recurrence; omitting row/column parity conditions for local-minimum starting points; boundary cells having fewer neighbors than interior cells. In the step-by-step conclusion, snake/spiral filling makes good-path starting points equal to local minima at even-even positions, with optimal count of the form ⌈n/2⌉² + ⌊n/2⌋² (e.g., 78² + 77² = 12013); DAG source counting proves the lower bound, and the first-order linear recurrence for independent sets along a path must clearly state initial values.
applicability: Counting strictly increasing sequences on paths or chessboards
Counting independent sets on paths
Chessboard path counting via snake/spiral filling
Reducing path counting to DAG source (local minimum) counting
Proving lower bounds via DAG source counting

steps.step: Set up the independent-set recurrence on a path
steps.detail: For a path with nodes, use a first-order linear recurrence based on the binary choice at each node: do not select the current node, or select the current node. If the current node is selected, the predecessor cannot be selected. Clearly state initial conditions: the empty graph case and the single-vertex case.

steps.step: Construct snake or spiral filling on the chessboard
steps.detail: Fill the chessboard in a snake or spiral pattern so that each cell has at most one incoming edge and one outgoing edge. This transforms the path-counting problem into counting sources (local minima) in a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

steps.step: Identify local-minimum starting points with parity conditions
steps.detail: Under the snake/spiral filling, good-path starting points correspond to local minima at even-even positions. Be careful to include row/column parity conditions and note that boundary cells have fewer neighbors than interior cells.

steps.step: Compute the optimal count and prove the lower bound
steps.detail: The optimal count takes the form ⌈n/2⌉² + ⌊n/2⌋² (for example, 78² + 77² = 12013). Use DAG source counting to prove the theoretical lower bound.

name: Density Guarantee and Expansion Frontier in Grid Growth Processes
description: When one party adds a bounded amount to a local neighborhood each round and the other party imposes a global bounded reduction each round, use a potential function defined as the ratio of net increment to affected area to prove a guaranteed lower bound on density. For diffusion-type growth problems, use the width of the expansion frontier to determine sparsity: if the frontier maintains two-dimensional expansion (its width reaches a fixed proportion of the board side length), growth is quadratic; otherwise it is confined to a one-dimensional strip and grows only linearly. The potential function is taken as (increment this round − opponent's reduction this round). The sparse threshold comes from converting the minimum width required to maintain a two-dimensional frontier into the board side length. Common pitfalls: mistaking the per-round upper bound for a total bound; miscalculating the influence of boundary neighborhoods (corner cells, edge cells); and confusing the conversion relation between frontier width and round number. The sparse threshold equals the critical initial amount required to maintain a two-dimensional frontier, of the form s = (side length)² − (⌊side length/2⌋ + 1)²; for example, with side length 75, s = 75² − 38² = 4181. Below this value the process is confined to a one-dimensional strip (O(n)); reaching it sustains Ω(n²) growth. The requested 'minimum non-sparse s' is the threshold itself, not the threshold minus one.
applicability: Grid or board growth processes with local addition versus global reduction per round
Diffusion-type expansion problems where frontier geometry determines growth rate
Problems requiring a guaranteed density lower bound under adversarial reduction
Determining whether growth is quadratic (two-dimensional) or linear (one-dimensional strip) based on frontier width

steps.detail: Let the potential function be the ratio of net increment to affected area. Concretely, for a given round, set Φ = (increment this round − opponent's reduction this round) / (area influenced by the operation). Use Φ to track the guaranteed density lower bound over time.

Measure the width of the expansion frontier. If the frontier width reaches a fixed proportion of the board side length n, the frontier is two-dimensional and growth is quadratic. If the frontier remains narrow (width bounded independently of n), growth is confined to a one-dimensional strip.

The critical threshold separating one-dimensional and two-dimensional growth is s = n² − (⌊n/2⌋ + 1)². For example, when n = 75, s = 75² − 38² = 4181. If the initial amount is below this threshold, the process is trapped in a one-dimensional strip with O(n) growth; if it reaches or exceeds this threshold, Ω(n²) growth can be maintained.
When asked for the minimum non-sparse s, return the threshold s itself. Do not return s − 1; the threshold is the smallest value that guarantees two-dimensional expansion.

steps.step: Watch for boundary and accounting pitfalls
steps.detail: Do not mistake the per-round upper bound for a total bound over all rounds. Carefully account for boundary neighborhoods: corner cells and edge cells have smaller affected areas than interior cells, which changes the potential function calculation. Also ensure the correct conversion between frontier width and round number is used.

name: Extremal Combinatorics: Double Counting and Turán-type Lower Bounds
description: For propositions asserting that 'any coloring or any sufficiently dense graph must contain a certain large structure', use double counting and the power mean (Hölder) inequality to establish a lower bound: the number of specified well-intersecting structures on a graph equals a convex estimate of the power sum of degrees. For coloring problems, use the pigeonhole principle and periodic (Latin-square-type) constructions to show that 'any small region contains all colors', thereby proving the bound is tight. The solution route writes the target quantity as 'sum over inner layer then raise to a power' before applying convexity inequalities; the upper-bound construction uses periodic coloring so that no small structure lacks any color. Common pitfalls include double-counting the same structure in double counting, reversing the direction of the power mean inequality, and failing to verify that the edge-count lower bound matches the extremal construction. Specifically, any k-coloring must contain a polyomino of area at least 2(k−1)² missing at least one color (pigeonhole + isoperimetric); a k-order periodic Latin-square coloring proves that any smaller area must contain all colors ⇒ extremal value = 2(k−1)² (e.g., 36 colors → 2450). Turán-type lower bounds use convexity estimates of degree power sums.
applicability: Problems asserting that any coloring or any dense graph must contain a certain large structure
Establishing lower bounds via double counting and power mean (Hölder) inequality
Coloring problems where periodic (Latin-square-type) constructions show tightness
Deriving Turán-type lower bounds from convexity of degree power sums

steps.step: Express the target quantity as a power of an inner sum
steps.detail: Write the quantity to be bounded in the form (∑_{inner} ...)^p so that convexity inequalities can be applied. Ensure the expression counts the specified well-intersecting structures on the graph.

steps.step: Apply double counting and convexity estimates
steps.detail: Use double counting to relate the number of structures to degree sequences. Then apply the power mean (Hölder) inequality to obtain a convex estimate of the power sum of degrees. Be careful not to reverse the inequality direction and avoid counting the same structure twice.

steps.step: Construct periodic colorings for upper bounds
steps.detail: Design a periodic coloring (e.g., Latin-square-type) such that any small structure contains all colors. This demonstrates that the lower bound cannot be improved without violating the construction.

steps.step: Verify matching of lower bound and extremal construction
steps.detail: Check that the edge-count or area lower bound matches the periodic construction. For k colors, the extremal polyomino area is exactly 2(k−1)²; for example, with 36 colors this gives 2450.

steps.step: Apply Turán-type convexity estimates for graphs
steps.detail: For graph problems, use convexity of degree power sums to derive Turán-type lower bounds on the number of specified substructures.

name: Counting on Symmetric Grids via Orbit Parameterization
description: When counting objects on symmetric grids (including triangular lattices and 3D cubic lattices), first parameterize the objects by their symmetry properties. On a triangular grid, a regular hexagon is determined by its side length and center position, where centers fall into two types: grid points and cell centers. On a 3D grid, unit cells are partitioned into orbit classes based on the equality pattern among their coordinates (all equal, exactly two equal, all distinct) combined with the parity of coordinate permutations. The total count then reduces to summing over parameters and orbit representatives. Warnings: (1) Do not miss objects in special rotation orientations (e.g., skewed regular hexagons); (2) Avoid double-counting orbit classes; (3) Carefully bound parameter ranges (e.g., maximum side length). For 3D coloring problems, a global constraint such as identical color multisets across three directional slices forces colors to lie only at the intersections of these slices and couples them together; cells are NOT independently colored. Whenever a proposed answer has the form n³ or similar power law, first verify by brute-force enumeration for n=2 and n=3; if the enumeration disagrees with the power formula, the modeling is wrong before extrapolating.
applicability: Counting regular hexagons on triangular grids including all rotation orientations
Counting or coloring unit cells on 3D cubic lattices under coordinate-equality and permutation-parity classification
Problems where global slice constraints couple cell colors rather than allowing independent choices
Small-n calibration (n=2,3) required before accepting closed-form power-law answers

steps.step: Parameterize hexagons on the triangular grid
steps.detail: Identify each regular hexagon by its side length s and its center type (grid point or cell center). Determine the legal range of s and center positions for the given board. Sum over all valid (s, center-type) pairs. The total count of regular hexagons over all rotation orientations on a triangular board of size n satisfies Σ s³ = (n(n+1)/2)², i.e., the square of the nth triangular number. Do not restrict to axis-aligned hexagons only.

steps.step: Classify 3D cells by coordinate equality pattern
steps.detail: For an n×n×n cubic lattice, partition cells according to the relations among coordinates (x,y,z): (i) all equal: x=y=z, contributing n cells; (ii) exactly two equal: patterns such as x=y≠z, x=z≠y, y=z≠x, contributing 3·C(n,2) cells; (iii) all distinct: x,y,z all different. For the all-distinct class, further split by the parity (even/odd) of the permutation ordering the coordinates, contributing 2·C(n,3) cells when counting orbit representatives under coordinate permutation.

steps.step: Handle coloring constraints via intersection coupling
steps.detail: If the problem imposes that the color multisets of three directional slices are identical, then colors can only appear at the triple intersections of these slices. Cells are not independently colored; the choices are coupled across the three directions. Model the count accordingly rather than multiplying independent per-cell color choices.

steps.step: Calibrate with small n and then scale
steps.detail: Use small values (e.g., n=2,3) for brute-force calibration to verify the orbit decomposition and any proposed closed form. If a formula such as n³ disagrees with the brute-force count, discard the model. Once verified, substitute the actual problem size n into the summed expression to obtain the final numerical answer. Do not report the small-n calibration value as the final answer.

name: Constrained Domino Covering Counting and Forced Uniqueness
description: This strategy addresses constrained domino placement on a chessboard where the set of uncovered squares satisfies a row/column condition: within each small square group, uncovered squares lie in the same row or same column. This constraint implies that the uncovered square set corresponds to a 'row-column selection' structure—selecting several rows and several columns whose intersection points are exactly the uncovered squares. The counting problem thus reduces to a combinatorial binomial coefficient form. When forcing a unique covering using marked squares, the role of the marks is to destroy all flippable alternating cycles; the required number of marks is of the same order as the board side length. Common pitfalls include: omitting the equivalence derivation between the constraint and the 'diagonal uncovered' pattern; claiming uniqueness without fully destroying all flippable alternating cycles; and failing to investigate discrepancies between small-scale enumeration and the general formula.
applicability: Constrained domino covering problems where uncovered squares satisfy same-row/same-column conditions within groups
Problems where the uncovered set forms an intersection structure of selected rows and columns
Forcing uniqueness of covering by placing marked squares to break alternating cycles
Calibration using small-scale brute-force values (k=1,2) to verify combinatorial formulas

steps.step: Translate constraints into geometric shape characterization of uncovered squares
steps.detail: Interpret the constraint that uncovered squares in each small group satisfy same-row/same-column condition. Derive that the uncovered square set must form a structure equivalent to selecting k rows and k columns, with the uncovered squares being exactly the k×k intersection points. Verify the equivalence direction carefully to avoid omitting the diagonal uncovered pattern derivation.

steps.step: Express the counting formula in closed combinatorial form
steps.detail: Given the row-column selection structure with k rows and k selected from a 2k×2k board (or equivalent dimension), the number of valid coverings is given by the squared binomial coefficient C(2k,k)². This is a combinatorial square form, not a linear expression. Report the answer as this combinatorial expression or its numerical value; linear forms of type 2(k+1) are prohibited.

For k=1, the brute-force count is 4; for k=2, the brute-force count is 36. These values must match the formula C(2k,k)²: C(2,1)² = 2² = 4 ✓; C(4,2)² = 6² = 36 ✓. If small-scale enumeration disagrees with the formula, investigate the discrepancy rather than ignoring it.

steps.step: Force uniqueness by destroying flippable alternating cycles
steps.detail: To enforce a unique covering, place marked squares that break all flippable alternating cycles (also called flip cycles or swap cycles). The number of marks required scales with the board side length (same order). Do not claim uniqueness unless all such cycles are confirmed destroyed.

name: Combinatorial Counting for the Circular Name-Tag Passing Game
description: This strategy counts the number of initial permutations of name tags on a round table such that after several rounds of the game, at least one player remains seated. The game proceeds by the rule: in each round, any player currently holding their own name tag leaves the table; the remaining players then pass their name tags one position to the left; and the circle contracts to close the gaps. The core method transforms the condition 'someone remains after r rounds' into 'the initial effective distance of that person's name tag exceeds r rounds'. The 'shrinking circle model' is used to recalculate passing steps according to the effective distance after each contraction. Counting is performed via combinatorial recurrences or inclusion-exclusion. Small-scale enumeration (n ≤ 10) is required to calibrate the model before extrapolating to larger scales using Eulerian numbers or the shrinking-circle recurrence; closed-form guessing is explicitly prohibited. Common pitfalls include miscalculating effective distance after adjacency changes due to contraction, confusing uniform counting with probability, and misordering the leave-and-pass sequence.
applicability: Counting initial permutations where at least one player remains seated after a specified number of rounds in the circular name-tag passing game.
Problems where the circle contracts after each round and passing direction is to the left among remaining players.
Scenarios where the condition can be expressed as initial effective distance of a name tag exceeding the number of rounds.
Small-scale calibration (n ≤ 10) followed by recurrence-based or inclusion-exclusion extrapolation to larger n.

steps.step: Define the game state and effective distance
steps.detail: Let n players be seated on a circle with a permutation π of name tags. In round t, any player i holding their own name tag (i.e., π(i) = i in the current configuration) leaves. The remaining players pass their name tags one position to the left along the current circle, and the circle contracts. Define the effective distance d(i) of player i's name tag as the number of left-passing steps required for that name tag to reach player i under the contraction dynamics. The condition that player i remains after r rounds is equivalent to d(i) > r.

steps.step: Calibrate the shrinking circle model via small-scale enumeration
steps.detail: For n ≤ 10, exhaustively simulate all n! initial permutations under the leave-pass-contract rules. For each permutation, record which players remain after r rounds and compute their initial effective distances. Verify that 'player i remains after r rounds' if and only if the initial effective distance of i's name tag exceeds r. Use this to validate the shrinking-circle distance recalculation formula and to catch errors in adjacency updates after contraction.

steps.step: Formulate the counting via recurrence or inclusion-exclusion
steps.detail: Let A(n, r) be the number of permutations of n players where everyone leaves within r rounds (i.e., all effective distances ≤ r). Then the desired count is n! − A(n, r). Compute A(n, r) using a recurrence derived from the shrinking circle model: after the first round, k players leave (those with fixed points in the current circle), and the remaining n−k players form a contracted circle with updated effective distances. Alternatively, apply inclusion-exclusion over the set of players whose effective distance exceeds r. The recurrence must account for the left-passing direction and the contraction-induced reindexing.

steps.step: Extrapolate to the target scale using Eulerian numbers or the validated recurrence
steps.detail: If the recurrence structure matches a known Eulerian number distribution (e.g., counting permutations by effective distance or displacement), use the Eulerian number closed form or recurrence. Otherwise, extend the validated shrinking-circle recurrence to the given n and r. Do not guess a closed form without prior small-n verification. Ensure boundary conditions are handled: if r ≥ n−1, typically everyone leaves; if r = 0, count permutations with at least one fixed point.

steps.step: Verify parity, boundary, and ordering constraints
steps.detail: Check that the leave-and-pass order is correctly modeled: leaving happens before passing in each round. Verify that effective distances are recomputed after each contraction, not using the original circle indices. Confirm that the counting is over permutations (uniform counting), not probabilities. Test edge cases: n=1, n=2, r=0, and r ≥ n.

name: Lempel-Ziv Dictionary Encoding
description: Lempel-Ziv (LZ) encoding decomposes a message into a phrase sequence of the form "previously seen phrase + new character", where each phrase is represented as a (dictionary index, character) pair. The dictionary is dynamically expanded during the encoding process. Finally, the index and character are concatenated into an encoded bit string according to a given fixed-length character mapping. The solution route uses greedy character-by-character matching of the longest previously seen prefix; the codeword is formed by concatenating the binary representation of the index with the binary representation of the character. Note that the number of index bits may change as the dictionary size grows. Common pitfalls include: greedy matching being too long so that the next phrase cannot be matched; inconsistent index numbering starting point (0 vs 1); and fixed-length codeword bit-width conventions. For step-by-step completion, the encoding output must provide, phrase by phrase, the concatenated bit string of 'dictionary index binary (fixed 3 bits) + character code (3 bits)', with indices starting from 0. Providing only the phrase decomposition earns partial credit; the complete bit string is the full answer.
applicability: Lossless compression of sequences via dynamic dictionary construction
Problems requiring explicit bit-string output from LZ phrase decomposition
Tasks where dictionary indices start at 0 and use fixed 3-bit binary representation
Tasks where character codes use fixed 3-bit binary representation

steps.step: Initialize the dictionary and read the input sequence
steps.detail: Start with an empty or predefined dictionary. Read the input sequence character by character. The dictionary will be populated dynamically with phrases as encoding proceeds.

For the current position in the sequence, find the longest phrase that already exists in the dictionary by extending character by character. Let this matched phrase be P and the next (new) character be c. The phrase to encode is (P, c). Note: Over-greedy matching may cause the subsequent phrase to become unmatchable, so verify that the remainder of the sequence can still be parsed.

steps.step: Assign dictionary index and output the codeword
steps.detail: Let the index of phrase P in the dictionary be i (starting from 0). The codeword for this phrase is formed by concatenating the binary representation of index i (fixed 3 bits) with the binary representation of character c (fixed 3 bits, according to the given character mapping). Output this 6-bit concatenated string as part of the final answer.

Add the new phrase (P concatenated with c, i.e., the matched phrase plus the new character) to the dictionary with the next available index. Advance the current position in the sequence past the matched phrase P and the character c. Repeat the process until the entire sequence is consumed.

Concatenate all phrase codewords in order to form the complete encoded bit string. Remember: only the phrase decomposition earns partial credit; the full bit string is required for complete credit. Ensure indices are 0-based and both index and character fields use the specified fixed 3-bit widths.

name: Arithmetic-Harmonic Mean Iteration and Fractional Linear Transformation
description: For a pair of coprime positive integers generating a reciprocal pair, repeatedly apply the arithmetic mean and harmonic mean to determine whether 1 can be generated in finitely many steps. The necessary and sufficient condition is: both numbers are odd and their sum is a power of 2. The core tool is the fractional linear transformation s = (x-1)/(x+1), which simultaneously converts the arithmetic mean and harmonic mean into rational function operations and reveals the invariant: the 'odd part' of the reduced denominator of all reachable values remains unchanged. The target value 1 corresponds to s = 0, so reachability requires the denominator of the initial s to be a power of 2, i.e., the sum of the two numbers is a power of 2. The construction (sufficiency) is completed by iteratively approaching via averaging; necessity is given by the odd-part invariant. Common pitfalls: verifying only the sufficiency construction without proving necessity; forgetting that the odd part remains invariant after reduction; omitting the condition that both numbers are odd; misusing the coprime condition causing the reduction conclusion to fail. After proving 'both numbers are odd and m+n is a power of 2', one must conclude: within the problem's range, take the largest/smallest power of 2 satisfying the condition (e.g., within upper bound 3000, the maximum sum is 2^11 = 2048), and give an explicit iterative path verification for (m,n) = (2^k+1, 2^k-1) to confirm reachability.
applicability: Problems involving 'arithmetic mean/harmonic mean (or general fractional linear operations) gradually generating a target value'
'Maximum feasible sum' and 'minimum unreachable' type problems often reduce to scanning in the sequence of powers of 2

steps.step: Identify the operation structure and apply the linearizing transformation
steps.detail: When encountering a problem where arithmetic mean and harmonic mean (or general fractional linear operations) are applied iteratively to generate a target value, first seek a transformation that diagonalizes or linearizes the operation. Use the fractional linear transformation s = (x-1)/(x+1). Under this transformation, the arithmetic mean and harmonic mean operations are simultaneously converted into rational function operations, making the invariant structure visible.

The key invariant revealed by the transformation is: the odd part of the reduced denominator of all reachable values remains unchanged. That is, after reducing each reachable value to lowest terms, the odd part of its denominator is constant throughout the iteration. The target value 1 corresponds to s = 0, whose denominator is 1 (a power of 2). Therefore, reachability requires that the denominator of the initial s be a power of 2.

steps.step: Derive the necessary and sufficient condition
steps.detail: From the invariant, deduce the necessary and sufficient condition for 1 to be reachable in finitely many steps: the two initial coprime positive integers must both be odd, and their sum must be a power of 2. Necessity follows from the odd-part invariance: if the sum is not a power of 2, the initial denominator has a nontrivial odd part that can never become 1. Sufficiency is established by explicit construction.

steps.step: Construct the explicit iterative path for sufficiency
steps.detail: For the pair (m,n) = (2^k+1, 2^k-1), which are coprime, both odd, and sum to 2^{k+1} (a power of 2), provide an explicit iterative path using repeated arithmetic and harmonic means to verify that 1 is indeed reachable. This confirms the sufficiency direction constructively.

After proving the condition 'both numbers are odd and m+n is a power of 2', one must finalize within the problem's stated range: select the largest or smallest power of 2 satisfying the condition. For example, if the upper bound is 3000, the maximum feasible sum is 2^11 = 2048. Then exhibit the corresponding (m,n) pair and its explicit iterative path to confirm reachability under the given constraints.

name: LCM-GCD Partition Density and Construction
description: For a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers, a cut position is called good if the least common multiple (LCM) of all elements in the front group equals the greatest common divisor (GCD) of all elements in the rear group. Local structure lemma: any three consecutive cut positions cannot all be good—if cut positions k, k+1, and k+2 are all good, it forces two adjacent terms to be equal, contradicting strict increase (note that two consecutive good cuts can occur). Consequently, the density upper bound for good cuts among all cut positions is at most two out of every three consecutive positions; the refined result states the maximum number of good cuts is approximately two-thirds of the total number of cut positions. When solving for the shortest sequence length that has exactly a given number of good cuts, first use the density upper bound to derive a lower bound on the length, then explicitly construct a sequence achieving that count via an LCM-based recursive assignment. Warning: do not confuse the assignment direction (front group uses LCM, rear group uses GCD); ignore boundary effects at endpoints at your peril as they cause counting errors; and ensure strict increase is maintained during construction.
applicability: Partition problems where front-group LCM equals rear-group GCD in strictly increasing positive integer sequences
Bounding or counting good cut positions via local density arguments
Finding the shortest sequence length that realizes exactly a specified number of good cuts
Constructive extremal sequence design using LCM recurrence

steps.detail: Given a strictly increasing sequence a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_n of positive integers, a cut after position k (1 ≤ k < n) is good if lcm(a_1, a_2, ..., a_k) = gcd(a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}, ..., a_n).

Show that three consecutive cut positions k, k+1, k+2 cannot all be good. Assuming all three are good yields equalities that force a_{k+1} = a_{k+2} or similar adjacent equality, violating strict increase. Hence among any three consecutive cut positions, at most two are good. Note that two consecutive good cuts are possible.

steps.step: Derive the global density upper bound
steps.detail: From the lemma, the number of good cuts is bounded by roughly two-thirds of the total number of cut positions. If there are n−1 cut positions, the maximum number of good cuts is approximately ⌊2(n−1)/3⌋ or its ceiling depending on endpoint behavior; use this to obtain a lower bound on n when a target count of good cuts is given.

steps.step: Construct a sequence achieving the bound
steps.detail: Use an explicit LCM-recursive assignment: build the sequence term by term so that prescribed cut positions become good while preserving strict increase. Typically set later terms as multiples of the running LCM to control the rear-group GCD and maintain the required equalities at the chosen good cuts.

steps.step: Verify strict increase and endpoint conditions
steps.detail: Check that a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_n holds throughout the constructed sequence, and carefully count good cuts near the first and last positions to avoid boundary-induced off-by-one errors.

name: Rich Set Integer Root Closure
description: A subset S of integers is called rich if for any polynomial with coefficients in S, all integer roots of that polynomial also belong to S. If S additionally contains all elements of the form 2^m - 2^n (differences of powers of 2), then S must contain all powers of 2, 0, and ±1. Using closure under integer roots of linear polynomials ax - b where a,b ∈ S and a|b, we obtain quotients b/a ∈ S. Combined with signed binary expansion representation of arbitrary integers using ±1 and powers of 2, induction shows S contains all integers. Thus the only rich set containing all differences of powers of 2 is Z itself.
applicability: Problems about sets closed under integer roots of polynomials with coefficients in the set
Sets containing differences of powers of 2 (2^m - 2^n)
Proving uniqueness of closed sets via propagation from seed elements
Problems requiring conversion of infinite set characterization to finite numerical answer (e.g., count of parameters or set size)

steps.step: Verify seed elements from differences of powers of 2
steps.detail: Given S contains all elements of form 2^m - 2^n for nonnegative integers m,n. Setting m=n gives 0 ∈ S. Setting m=n+1 gives 2^{n+1} - 2^n = 2^n ∈ S, so all powers of 2 are in S. Then 2^1 - 2^0 = 1 ∈ S and 2^0 - 2^1 = -1 ∈ S, so ±1 ∈ S.

steps.step: Apply linear polynomial closure for divisibility
steps.detail: For any a,b ∈ S with a ≠ 0 and a dividing b, the linear polynomial ax - b has coefficients in S and integer root x = b/a. By rich set definition, b/a ∈ S. Thus S is closed under division when the divisor divides the dividend.

steps.step: Generate all integers via signed binary expansion
steps.detail: Any integer k can be written as k = Σ ε_i 2^i where ε_i ∈ {−1,0,1} (signed binary expansion). Since ±1 ∈ S and all powers of 2 ∈ S, and S is closed under addition of elements (via constructing appropriate polynomials or iterative closure), all such sums belong to S. Hence Z ⊆ S.

steps.step: Conclude uniqueness and extract numerical answer
steps.detail: Since S ⊆ Z by definition and Z ⊆ S, we have S = Z. When the problem asks for a specific quantity (e.g., number of such sets, size of a finite parameterization, etc.), substitute S = Z back into the problem statement to obtain a finite numerical answer, not ∞.

name: Binary carry structure and 2-adic valuation for Frobenius-type nonrepresentability
description: Two main threads centered on powers of 2: (a) For a generating set consisting of n elements each being a difference of powers of 2 (each element has a binary pattern of a block of consecutive 1s followed by a block of 0s, with total bit length exactly n), study the range of integers covered by nonnegative linear combinations (repetition allowed) of these elements. The maximum element is 2^n - 1, the gcd of the set is 1, hence all sufficiently large integers are representable. The largest nonrepresentable integer takes the form (linear factor) × (power of 2) + 1. The proof relies on the carry structure of binary addition—each generator contributes a block of consecutive 1s, and the interaction between superposition and carries determines the boundary between representable and nonrepresentable numbers. (b) The odd part function f(n) = n / 2^m (where m is the exponent of the highest power of 2 dividing n) always takes odd values. Its value modulo a given number is determined by the depth of divisibility by 2: when n is odd it is n itself; when n contains powers of 2, repeatedly divide out those factors and then take modulo. Requiring that the differences of function values of several consecutive terms in an interval are all multiples of a given modulus is equivalent to f modulo that modulus exhibiting a periodic structure on that interval; when the period length itself contains a power of 2, it conflicts with deeper 2-adic structure, and careful adjustment can compress feasible parameters to very few candidate values.
applicability: Frobenius-type problems where generators have neat binary patterns of consecutive 1s followed by 0s with total bit length n
Problems involving the odd part function f(n) = n / 2^m and its periodicity modulo a given number
Cases where the largest nonrepresentable integer is expected to take the form (linear factor) × 2^k + 1
Situations requiring analysis of carry interactions in binary addition for representability
Problems where period length conflicts with 2-adic depth, requiring layered elimination of candidates

steps.detail: For a generating set with n elements, each element is a difference of powers of 2 with binary representation consisting of a block of consecutive 1s followed by a block of 0s, total bit length exactly n. The maximum element is 2^n - 1. Verify that gcd of the set is 1, ensuring all sufficiently large integers are representable.

Each generator contributes a block of consecutive 1s in binary. When forming nonnegative linear combinations (with repetition allowed), the superposition of these blocks and the resulting carry interactions determine which integers are representable. Use induction on the carry structure to characterize the boundary between representable and nonrepresentable numbers.

steps.step: Derive closed form for largest nonrepresentable integer
steps.detail: The largest nonrepresentable integer takes the form (linear factor) × 2^k + 1. Prove this by analyzing how carries propagate when adding generator patterns. Verify the formula with small values of n (calibration) to ensure boundary cases are handled correctly.

steps.step: Decompose odd part function by 2-adic depth
steps.detail: For f(n) = n / 2^m where m = v₂(n) (the 2-adic valuation), write f piecewise by the depth of divisibility by 2: if n is odd, f(n) = n; if n is divisible by 2^m but not 2^{m+1}, then f(n) = n / 2^m which is odd. Ensure no layers are confused and the modulus is correctly applied at each layer.

steps.step: Translate periodicity conditions to depth constraints
steps.detail: Requiring that differences of f values over consecutive terms are multiples of a modulus m is equivalent to f mod m being periodic on that interval. When the period length contains a power of 2, it conflicts with deeper 2-adic structure. Identify the obstruction at the layer v₂(n) = log₂v - 1, and eliminate infeasible parameters layer by layer.

steps.step: Compress to candidate set and verify
steps.detail: After layered elimination, feasible parameters are compressed to a small candidate set (e.g., of the form {1, 3, 5}). The answer is obtained by explicit verification of each remaining candidate. Do not skip verification of boundary cases where period length and 2-adic depth conflict.

name: Discriminant Perfect-Square Parameterization for Diophantine Equations
description: For parameterized Diophantine equations, a common method is to rewrite the equation as a quadratic in one variable and require its discriminant to be a perfect square. If the discriminant can be arranged as the square of a polynomial, one directly obtains a parametric family of solutions where the parameter ranges over positive integers; both construction and back-substitution verification are indispensable. If only the parity of the number of integer solutions is required, transform the perfect-square discriminant constraint into a quadratic-form/norm equation (studying representation numbers in an imaginary quadratic field); the parity of the number of solutions is then determined by the corresponding divisibility condition. The shared structure of such problems is: first use the non-negativity of the discriminant to bound the variable range or determine the shape of the parameter family, then refine via the perfect-square condition.
applicability: Parameterized Diophantine equations that can be rearranged into a quadratic equation in one variable
Problems asking for the parity (odd/even) of the number of ordered integer solutions
Equations with symmetric structure (e.g., two variables of the same degree) that can be paired and simplified

steps.step: Eliminate radicals and form a quadratic
steps.detail: For equations containing radicals, first move terms and square to remove radicals, obtaining a univariate quadratic equation in one variable.

steps.step: Compute the discriminant and impose perfect-square condition
steps.detail: Write the discriminant Δ of the quadratic. Require Δ to be a perfect square. If Δ can be expressed as the square of a polynomial in the parameter, say Δ = [P(t)]², then solve for the variable in terms of the parameter t to obtain a parametric family of solutions.

Substitute the parametric solutions back into the original equation to confirm they are genuine solutions; this step is indispensable to avoid extraneous solutions introduced by squaring or parameterization.

steps.step: Use discriminant non-negativity to bound variables
steps.detail: From Δ ≥ 0, derive the bounded range of the variable or the admissible shape of the parameter family before applying the perfect-square refinement.

When only the parity of the number of ordered integer solutions is needed, convert the condition 'Δ is a perfect square' into a quadratic-form or norm equation in an imaginary quadratic field. The parity of the number of representations is then decided by the corresponding divisibility condition, avoiding point-by-point enumeration.
If the equation has symmetric structure (e.g., two variables appear with the same degree), first pair symmetric terms to simplify the expression before applying the discriminant method.

name: Weight Function Invariant and Worst-Case Distribution Lower Bound
description: When moving pieces on a 3D grid toward the origin by repeatedly merging pieces along each coordinate axis using distinct merging bases and shifting one step in the negative direction, define a weight function for each point as the reciprocal of the product of powers of the merging bases: increasing the coordinate by 1 along an axis divides the weight by that axis's base. Each operation preserves the total weight sum. Since a single piece at the origin has weight 1, the initial total weight must be at least 1. The worst initial distribution piles all pieces at the farthest corner from the origin, yielding an exact lower bound on the minimum total number of pieces required to guarantee reachability; a greedy moving sequence can achieve this bound.
applicability: Process problems involving merging by different multiples and moving toward a fixed point
When merging bases are pairwise coprime integers, a weight function in the form of a product of powers naturally makes the operation conserved
The argument proceeds in two steps: necessity (weight sum invariant) and sufficiency (constructing reachability)

steps.step: Define the weight function on the 3D grid
steps.detail: Let the three coordinate axes have distinct merging bases a, b, c. For a grid point (x, y, z) with non-negative integer coordinates, define its weight as w(x, y, z) = 1/(a^x b^y c^z). Thus increasing a coordinate by 1 along an axis divides the weight by the corresponding base.

steps.step: Show the total weight sum is invariant under each operation
steps.detail: An operation merges pieces along one axis (say the x-axis) using base a and shifts them one step toward the negative direction. Because the weight function is defined as the reciprocal of the product of powers of the bases, the total weight sum before and after the operation remains unchanged. The same holds for operations along the y- and z-axes.

steps.step: Derive the necessary lower bound from the invariant
steps.detail: A single piece at the origin (0, 0, 0) has weight w(0, 0, 0) = 1. Since the total weight is invariant, any initial configuration that can eventually produce a piece at the origin must have total weight at least 1.

The worst distribution—requiring the largest number of pieces to achieve total weight ≥ 1—is to place all pieces at the farthest corner of the grid from the origin. This gives the exact lower bound on the minimum total number of pieces needed to guarantee reachability.

steps.step: Prove sufficiency by constructing a greedy sequence
steps.detail: A greedy merging-and-moving sequence (always merge when possible along any axis toward the origin) can achieve the lower bound derived from the worst-case distribution, proving the bound is tight.

name: Fibonacci and Lucas Identity-Based Minimal Difference Cover
description: Strategy for finding the smallest integer set whose pairwise differences cover all Fibonacci number differences over a given index interval (plus an accompanying Lucas number difference). Core identity: the difference of two consecutive even-index Fibonacci numbers equals the middle odd-index term, F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1}. Therefore, including 0 and all even-index Fibonacci numbers in the set allows adjacent differences to cover all target odd-index terms; Lucas numbers can also be rewritten as differences of two Fibonacci numbers. Minimality is derived from the fact that endpoint differences can only be expressed via adjacent even-index terms—removing the outermost elements makes the endpoint differences unrepresentable. Common pitfalls: forgetting the adjacent even-index difference identity; including odd-index terms in the set, making it larger than necessary; proving minimality by counting alone rather than by non-representability.
applicability: Problems involving Fibonacci/Lucas numbers where index parity-related identities are relevant
Problems requiring a set of integers whose differences cover a specified target set of values
Problems asking for the minimum/smallest/least such covering set

steps.step: List relevant Fibonacci and Lucas identities tied to index parity
steps.detail: Write down identities such as F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1} and expressions of Lucas numbers as differences of Fibonacci numbers. These connect even-index elements to the odd-index differences they must cover.

steps.step: Construct the candidate covering set using 0 and even-index Fibonacci numbers
steps.detail: Include 0 and all even-index Fibonacci numbers within the relevant index range. By the identity F_{2k} − F_{2k−2} = F_{2k−1}, adjacent differences in this set produce every required odd-index Fibonacci difference. Any required Lucas difference can also be represented as a difference of two Fibonacci numbers, hence covered by the set.

Show that the extreme (endpoint) differences can only be obtained from the outermost even-index elements. If the outermost element is removed, the corresponding endpoint difference becomes unrepresentable. Therefore no proper subset can still cover all required differences. Avoid relying solely on counting arguments.

name: Decimal Digit Operations and Divisibility Strategies
description: This module records two reusable strategies for decimal digit manipulation problems involving divisibility. (a) Distinct-digit 'deletion-divisible' numbers: starting from one-digit seeds, iteratively append digits to build larger numbers such that the new number is an integer multiple of the previous number and deleting one specific digit recovers the previous number. The deletion operation must not create leading zeros, and the resulting number must retain the distinct-digit property. The maximum such number is verified by an explicit deletion chain where each step removes some digit (the digit and position may vary per step) to obtain the number from the prior step. (b) Divisibility patterns of digit sums over consecutive integers: when no carry occurs, the digit sum modulo a given prime p increases by 1 at each step; when a carry occurs across a block of consecutive 9s, the digit sum drops sharply. Determining that 'every digit sum within a fixed-length segment is not divisible by p' is equivalent to avoiding intervals where the digit sum lands on a multiple of p. Minimality is verified via digit-sum dynamic programming or segment-by-segment scanning. General problem-solving route: for digit-operation problems, first clarify the legal rules for 'deleting a digit' (deleting the leading digit is forbidden if it creates a leading zero); the '+1 increment, sharp drop on carry' pattern of digit sums modulo p is the key tool for locating forbidden segments; 'product not divisible' should first be reduced to 'every factor is not divisible'.
applicability: Constructing or searching for distinct-digit numbers where deleting one digit yields a divisor of the original number, and the property can be iterated.
Verifying the maximum such number via an explicit deletion chain.
Analyzing whether digit sums of consecutive integers over a fixed interval are all not divisible by a given prime p.
Locating forbidden intervals where digit sum ≡ 0 (mod p) using the +1 increment and carry-drop pattern.
Reducing 'product not divisible by p' to checking each factor individually.

steps.detail: When deleting a digit from a decimal number, the operation is illegal if it creates a leading zero (e.g., deleting the first digit of a number whose second digit is 0). The resulting number must also preserve the distinct-digit property if required by the problem.

steps.step: Construct deletion-divisible numbers by iterative expansion
steps.detail: Start from one-digit seed numbers. For each current number n with distinct digits, try appending a digit d (0–9, not already in n) to form a new number n' such that n' is an integer multiple of n (i.e., n' = k·n for some integer k ≥ 2) and there exists a digit in n' whose deletion yields back n. Continue expanding until no further valid extension is possible. Use branching search (e.g., Python recursion/backtracking) rather than seeking a closed-form analytic expression.

steps.step: Verify the maximum deletion-divisible number via an explicit deletion chain
steps.detail: To confirm a candidate maximum number, exhibit a deletion chain: a sequence of numbers starting from the candidate down to a one-digit number, where each step deletes exactly one digit (digit and position may differ per step) to obtain the previous number. At every step verify (i) the divisibility relation (the larger number is a multiple of the smaller), and (ii) all digits in each number are distinct.

steps.step: Model digit sum modulo p behavior over consecutive integers
steps.detail: Let p be a given prime. When incrementing an integer by 1, if no carry occurs (i.e., the last digit is not 9), the digit sum increases by 1, so digit sum modulo p increases by 1 modulo p. If a carry occurs across a block of t consecutive trailing 9s, the digit sum drops by 9t – 1 (since the 9s become 0s and the digit before them increases by 1). This creates a sharp drop in the digit sum modulo p.

steps.step: Identify forbidden intervals for digit sum divisibility
steps.detail: A segment of consecutive integers all have digit sums not divisible by p if and only if the segment avoids all positions where the digit sum lands on a multiple of p. Scan the integer line segment by segment, using the +1 increment and carry-drop pattern to mark intervals where digit sum ≡ 0 (mod p); the complement gives the allowed segments.

steps.step: Verify minimality via digit-sum DP or segment scanning
steps.detail: To prove a certain length is minimal (e.g., the shortest interval guaranteeing a digit sum divisible by p), either run a digit-sum dynamic programming over the relevant range or scan consecutive blocks explicitly, checking that every shorter interval can avoid the forbidden multiples while the claimed length cannot.

steps.step: Reduce product non-divisibility to factor-wise checks
steps.detail: If a problem asks that a product of several integers is not divisible by a prime p, this is equivalent to requiring that none of the individual factors is divisible by p. Do not confuse 'product not divisible' with the negation of 'each factor divisible'.

name: Linear Programming Duality: Construction Rules and Duality Theorems
description: For a primal–dual pair in linear programming, construct the dual by transposing the constraint matrix, interchanging the objective coefficients and the right-hand sides of the constraints, and reversing the optimization direction: a minimization primal corresponds to a maximization dual. The dual of the dual returns to the primal. Weak duality states the ordering relation between the objective value of every dual-feasible solution and the optimal value, while strong duality states that the two problems have equal optimal values when the relevant optimal solutions exist. In multiple-choice questions, each statement about the dual construction must be checked separately and precisely.
applicability: A problem asks for the dual of a linear program or for a judgment about primal–dual conversion.
The question concerns the transpose of the constraint matrix, the destination of the right-hand side, objective coefficients, or the optimization direction.
Weak duality or strong duality is needed to compare feasible objective values or optimal values.

steps.step: Identify the primal matrix, coefficients, and optimization direction
steps.detail: Record the constraint matrix, the objective-function coefficient vector, the right-hand-side vector, the inequality directions, and whether the primal is a minimization or maximization problem.

steps.step: Construct the dual component by component
steps.detail: Transpose the constraint matrix; exchange the roles of the primal objective coefficients and constraint right-hand sides; and reverse the optimization direction, so a minimization primal has a maximization dual.
Verify that applying the construction a second time returns the original primal problem, including its matrix orientation, coefficients, directions, and optimization type.

steps.step: Apply weak and strong duality precisely
steps.detail: Use weak duality for the inequality between the objective value of a dual-feasible solution and the appropriate optimum, and use strong duality only for equality of the two optimal values under its conditions.

steps.step: Audit verbal statements one by one
steps.detail: Do not accept an imprecise claim such as ‘the objective function becomes a constraint.’ The primal objective coefficients become the right-hand sides of dual constraints; the primal constraint right-hand sides enter the dual objective; and the constraint matrix itself is transposed.

name: Translation-Invariant Total Orders and Parity Analysis of Rank Functions
description: A bijection with translation-order-preserving behavior is equivalent to a translation-invariant total order. Such an order is determined by a positive cone and can be represented as layers of a linear functional together with a tie-breaking rule inside every layer. Its rank function decomposes into a layer count plus an in-layer offset. This decomposition permits exact parity counting of ranks on a target rectangular region. One must range over the feasible parameter family consisting of coprime slopes and tie-breaking rules and optimize over that family. The count N varies with the coprime parameters (p,q) and the tie-breaking direction between N_min and N_max; the two extremes are attained by the two tie-breaking choices for an extreme slope of type (1,q). If the requested quantity is a product or combination of endpoint values, both endpoints must be found by traversing the parameter family rather than evaluating only one parameter choice.
applicability: A problem concerns an order-preserving bijection that is invariant under translations, or an equivalent translation-invariant total order.
The order is described by a coprime linear-functional slope (p,q) and an in-layer tie-breaking rule such as smaller x first versus smaller y first.
The task counts even or odd rank values on a rectangular target region, especially one with half-open interval boundaries.
The required result depends on extrema over all admissible order parameters.

steps.step: Replace the order-preserving bijection by a translation-invariant total order
steps.detail: Use the equivalence in the correct direction: the translation-order-preserving bijection induces a translation-invariant total order, and conversely the order determines the corresponding ranking behavior.

steps.step: Parameterize the order by layers and a tie-break
steps.detail: Choose a linear functional with coprime slope parameters (p,q), use its values as layer indices, and specify the in-layer rule, for example whether smaller x or smaller y is placed first.
Write each rank as the number of points in earlier layers plus the offset within the current layer. Keep these two terms separate when computing parity.

steps.step: Count parity by layer index and offset
steps.detail: For every point in the target rectangle, classify the parity of the layer contribution and the in-layer offset, then combine the two parities. Respect half-open boundary conventions exactly.

Compute the count for each admissible coprime slope and each tie-breaking direction. The values range from N_min to N_max, with endpoint values attained by the two tie-breaks for an extreme slope of type (1,q); do not infer the answer from a single parameter setting.

name: Digit DP for Divisibility Counting with Restricted Digit Sets
description: To count natural numbers whose number of digits is at most a specified bound, whose digits belong to a finite digit set, and whose value satisfies divisibility by a small modulus, use digit-by-digit dynamic programming. The state is the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or numerical value, and transitions are performed one digit at a time. Transition coefficients are determined by the residues modulo the modulus contributed by digits in the allowed set. The key distinction is between counting strings that allow leading zeroes and counting genuine natural numbers: the leading digit cannot be zero. The correction is: the number of valid natural numbers of length L equals the number of valid strings of length L minus the number of valid strings of length L−1. Finally, treat whether 0 itself is included according to the problem statement.
applicability: The three features ‘restricted digit set + divisibility by a small integer + bounded digit length’ occur together.
The modulus is small, often a one-digit integer, so remainder can be used directly as a DP-state dimension.
Several allowed digits can have the same residue modulo the modulus, allowing transitions to be compressed by residue frequency.

steps.detail: When the digit set is finite, the number must be divisible by a small modulus, and the number of digits has an upper bound, use a position-by-position DP rather than direct enumeration of strings.
Track the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or processed numerical value, using the update rule appropriate to the divisibility condition.

For every allowed digit, compute its residue modulo the modulus. If multiple digits have the same residue, count the number of occurrences of each residue first and use those counts as transition coefficients.

steps.step: Count strings with leading zeroes first
steps.detail: Run the DP for length L while allowing zero in every position to obtain the count of valid digit strings of length L.

Because the first digit of a natural number cannot be zero, use valid_natural_numbers(L) = valid_strings(L) − valid_strings(L−1). Sum the required lengths from 1 to the specified upper bound with correct endpoints.

Check separately whether 0 is included by the problem statement. Avoid direct string enumeration without remainder classes, omitted leading-zero correction, and off-by-one errors in the length summation.

name: Classification of Integer-Valued Functions Under Divisibility Constraints
description: If an integer-valued function g satisfies the condition that, for every pair of distinct integers a,b, the difference g(a)−g(b) divides the corresponding difference of powers, then all solutions have power-function-family form: g is x raised to the d-th power, where d ranges over the divisors of the specified positive integer, or a mirror/translation variant of such a power function. When the exponent and power satisfy particular parity conditions, there is an additional signed family. The number of functions is twice the number of divisors when the exponent contains no factor 2. When it contains a power-of-2 factor, writing the exponent as its 2-adic part times its odd part gives twice the product of twice the 2-adic exponent and the number of divisors of the odd part. The condition that this number is 2 times an odd integer is equivalent to the divisor count being odd, hence to the positive integer being a perfect square. Combined with the parity constraint, this frequently reduces to odd perfect squares.
applicability: An integer-valued function is constrained by divisibility of differences g(a)−g(b) by differences of powers for all distinct integers a,b.
The task requires classification of all functions, counting the families, or locating the N-th positive integer with a stated count property.
The exponent has parity or 2-adic structure relevant to the number of solution families.

steps.detail: Start from the power functions g(x)=x^d for every divisor d of the specified positive integer, together with their mirror/translation variants.
Analyze the specified parity relation between exponent and power. Include the additional signed solution family when that parity condition holds; do not omit it.
If the exponent has no factor 2, the total is 2 times the divisor count. If it has a 2-adic factor and an odd part, use 2 times twice the 2-adic exponent times the divisor count of the odd part.

steps.step: Convert the requested count property into a divisor property
steps.detail: Use count = 2 × odd if and only if the divisor count is odd, which holds if and only if the integer is a perfect square. Combine this with any parity restriction.

steps.step: Invert an ordinal only after deriving the sequence
steps.detail: For the resulting odd-perfect-square sequence, the N-th term is (2N−1)^2. Check N=1,2,3, obtaining 1,9,25, before substituting the requested ordinal; do not use N^2 directly.
